title: The Partial Testimony of Logs: Evaluation of Language Model Generation under Confounded Model Choice
venue_date: arXiv:2605.01311v1, cs.LG, submitted 2 May 2026. Jikai Jin, Vasilis Syrgkanis (Stanford).
what_it_does: The closest thing in the literature to an explicitly causal framing of an inference-time decision. Defines a do-calculus estimand for LM generation: marginal model value mu(a) = E[Y(do(A=a))] and context-conditional q(x,a) = E[Y(do(A=a))|X=x]. Identifies it from a three-source design: a confounded observational log (OBS), a small randomized experiment (EXP), and an offline simulator (SIM). Crucially, the TREATMENT is *model choice* (which generative model is deployed), NOT which candidate to return and NOT when to stop. Identification comes from EXP + SIM jointly; OBS is not required for identification. It does NOT use IPW or propensity scores — it conditions on (X,M) and uses EXP randomization to break the confounding path through latent user state.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: semi-synthetic CNN/DailyMail with smooth reward, average rank across settings — CVCI 2.04 (best), OBS-only 2.83, EXP-only 2.90. At n_OBS=20,000 / n_EXP=200, CVCI regret 0.0120 (best). Sample-size grid n_OBS in {2,000; 20,000}, n_EXP in {20; 200}. Real-task caches: CNN/DailyMail 48 articles x 20 models; SWE-bench Verified 500 issues with BouncerBench patches, outcomes = programmatic fix success c1 plus patch-quality features c2-c4. Coding result: representation-EXP wins when auxiliary patch features predict the target (alpha_fix < 0.25); OBS-based families dominate once true fix success dominates (alpha_fix > 0.25).
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED. There is no k (candidate count) at all — the action space is 20 models, not 20 draws from one model. No per-task draw budget is reported.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED. Model sizes are not the axis; the 20 models are API/cached endpoints and no parameter counts are given. No sub-8B analysis.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the paper that would occupy our framing if it went one step further, and it explicitly does not. Assumption A4 restricts the whole framework to 'single-round, stateless generation', and the paper states that in 'repeated, adaptive, or multi-round interactions the residual dependence of M on U given (X,A) is generally nonzero, so A4 fails.' So: (a) sequential/multi-round treatments are named and excluded; (b) the treatment is model choice, not selection-among-candidates or stopping; (c) the design is observational-log-plus-small-EXP, i.e. it solves confounding, whereas we propose PROSPECTIVE randomization with KNOWN propensities, which sidesteps the problem this paper works hard on. Our niche survives. Practical consequence: we should cite this as the single nearest neighbour and position against it on exactly those three axes, and we should note that its SWE-bench section already normalizes programmatic outcomes as the reward in causal LM evaluation — that part of our novelty is gone.

title: DOCE: Finding the Sweet Spot for Execution-Based Code Generation
venue_date: arXiv:2408.13745v4, 16 October 2024 (v4). arXiv preprint.
what_it_does: The single most decision-relevant paper for the execution-agreement question, because it is the only one that (i) uses sub-8B code models, (ii) uses HumanEval+ and MBPP-S+ (our benchmarks), and (iii) separately reports the visible-test FILTER, execution-agreement MBR-Exec, and their combination against the ORACLE pass@n. MBR-Exec clusters candidates by execution outputs on common inputs and picks the lowest-Bayes-risk (largest-agreement) candidate. Filtering = discard any candidate that fails the trial unit tests given in the prompt/docstring, i.e. exactly our 'visible assertion passes' rule.
key_numbers:
ALL MEASURED-IN-PAPER, n=50 candidates, Table 1.
DeepSeekCoder-6.7B-Instruct, MBPP-S+: Random 58.6 / Greedy 64.3 / LL 58.9 / Filter 72.6 / Filter+LL 72.8 / MBR-Exec 78.6 / Filter+MBR-Exec 82.1 / Oracle pass@50 85.6.
DeepSeekCoder-6.7B-Instruct, HumanEval+: Random 65.1 / Greedy 76.8 / LL 71.8 / Filter 78.7 / Filter+LL 79.1 / MBR-Exec 85.5 / Filter+MBR-Exec 89.8 / Oracle 93.2.
CodeLlama-7B-Instruct, HumanEval+: Random 30.2 / Greedy 39.0 / LL 38.7 / Filter 59.7 / Filter+LL 60.4 / MBR-Exec 49.5 / Filter+MBR-Exec 70.1 / Oracle 76.2.
CodeLlama-7B-Instruct, MBPP-S+: Random 41.9 / Greedy 44.8 / LL 42.6 / Filter 60.8 / Filter+LL 59.7 / MBR-Exec 57.8 / Filter+MBR-Exec 69.3 / Oracle 72.0.
INFERRED — fraction of the FILTER-to-ORACLE gap that execution agreement recovers (this is our estimand, because Filter is our 0.7455 baseline and Oracle is our 0.8192): DeepSeek-6.7B MBPP-S+ (82.1-72.6)/(85.6-72.6) = 9.5/13.0 = 73.1%. DeepSeek-6.7B HumanEval+ 11.1/14.5 = 76.6%. CodeLlama-7B HumanEval+ 10.4/16.5 = 63.0%. CodeLlama-7B MBPP-S+ 8.5/11.2 = 75.9%. Range 63.0-76.6%, mean 72.2%.
INFERRED — agreement WITHOUT the visible filter, greedy-to-oracle: CodeLlama-7B HumanEval+ (49.5-39.0)/(76.2-39.0) = 28.2%; DeepSeek-6.7B MBPP-S+ (78.6-64.3)/(85.6-64.3) = 67.1%.
INFERRED — log-likelihood selection recovers essentially nothing on top of the filter: Filter+LL minus Filter = +0.7, +0.4, +0.7, -1.1 pp across the four cells, i.e. 5.4%, 2.8%, 4.2%, -9.8% of the filter-to-oracle gap.
small_k_evidence: PARTIAL AND FIGURE-ONLY. The paper sweeps n = {5,10,15,20,25,30,40,50} but I confirmed there is NO appendix table of values at n=5 or n=10 — only Figure 4 / Figures 7-8 curves. Read off those figures (APPROXIMATE, not MEASURED): CodeLlama-7B-Instruct HumanEval+ at n=5, MBR-Exec without filtering ~35, with filtering ~55; at n=10, ~40 and ~58, with oracle@10 ~68. DeepSeekCoder-6.7B-Instruct HumanEval+ with filtering ~82 at n=5 and ~85 at n=10, oracle@10 ~92. The only explicit prose claim is directional: 'with filtering, MBR-Exec shows considerable improvements over the case without filtering, with performance scaling much better with more candidates' — i.e. the paper tells us the method is BETTER at large n and gives us no trustworthy number at n<=10.
small_model_evidence: YES, the best in the literature: CodeLlama-7B-Instruct and DeepSeekCoder-6.7B-Instruct are both under 8B, and both are evaluated on HumanEval+ and MBPP-S+ with EvalPlus hidden tests. Larger comparators are CodeLlama-13B and DeepSeekCoder-V2-Lite-16B. No 3B model is tested — our Qwen2.5-3B is below everything in this paper.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the number that decides whether execution agreement is worth 5 hours of M5 time, and it says yes with two large caveats. (1) The positive read: on sub-8B models, on our exact two benchmarks, with hidden-test grading, execution agreement recovers 63-77% of the visible-filter-to-oracle gap. Applied to our 3B gap of 0.0737 that is +0.046 to +0.057 absolute (0.792-0.803), and to our 7B gap of 0.0351 it is +0.022 to +0.027 — both far above the zero our static-feature GBM and logistic models returned. (2) Caveat that must be stated in our writeup: DOCE's MBR-Exec 'use[s] all unit tests given but only their inputs', i.e. it executes candidates on the INPUTS OF THE EVALUATION TESTS. Under our strict visible/hidden split that information does not exist for the selector, so DOCE's 63-77% is an UPPER BOUND for us, not an estimate. The paper itself concedes this: 'it requires access to execution unit test inputs, which is impractical'. Our version must self-generate inputs, and H4 quantifies what that costs. (3) The n=50 vs our k<=8 mismatch is real and the paper's own prose says the method scales with n, so the curve is rising where we would sit. (4) A free gift: Filter+LL adds 3-5% of the gap, which independently reproduces our null on cheap non-execution features and is worth citing as external corroboration of our own negative result.

title: CodeT: Code Generation with Generated Tests
venue_date: arXiv:2207.10397, ICLR 2023. Microsoft Research.
what_it_does: The canonical dual-execution-agreement paper, and — critically for us — the one that benchmarks PURE execution-output clustering as a named ablation. AlphaCode-C is their reimplementation of exactly the method we propose (run candidates on common inputs, take the largest output-agreement cluster). CodeT itself is stronger: it scores consensus sets by both the number of passing generated test cases and the number of agreeing solutions, RANSAC-style, so it needs generated tests WITH expected outputs, not just common inputs.
key_numbers:
MEASURED-IN-PAPER, n=100 candidate samples on HumanEval and MBPP, pass@1.
InCoder-6B (6.7B, under 8B) HumanEval: baseline 16.4 / AlphaCode-C 17.7 / CodeT 20.6.
InCoder-6B MBPP: baseline 21.3 / AlphaCode-C 26.7 / CodeT 34.4.
CodeGen-Mono-16B HumanEval: baseline 29.7 / AlphaCode-C 27.3 / CodeT 36.7.
CodeGen-Mono-16B MBPP: baseline 42.4 / AlphaCode-C 41.0 / CodeT 49.5.
INFERRED — pure agreement clustering (AlphaCode-C) vs baseline: HumanEval InCoder-6B +1.3pp, CodeGen-16B -2.4pp; MBPP InCoder-6B +5.4pp, CodeGen-16B -1.4pp. So on 2 of 4 cells pure clustering is NEGATIVE. INFERRED — AlphaCode-C captures only 5.4/13.1 = 41.2% of CodeT's MBPP gain on InCoder-6B and 1.3/4.2 = 31.0% of it on HumanEval. Oracle pass@n is NOT REPORTED in the rows I could verify, so a gap-fraction against oracle is NOT FOUND for this paper.
small_k_evidence: NONE. This is the trap: CodeT's ablation Table 4 sweeps 10/20/50/100 TEST CASES, not candidates. The candidate count is fixed at n=100 for HumanEval/MBPP (n=50 APPS, n=1000 CodeContests) throughout. There is no k<=10 candidate result anywhere in the paper.
small_model_evidence: One sub-8B model: InCoder-6B (6.7B params). Nothing at 3B. The paper does note that 'smaller models show larger absolute improvements from CodeT', which is weakly encouraging for our 3B.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the strongest piece of evidence AGAINST our specific untested candidate, and it should change our plan. The exact method we named — 'run every candidate on common inputs and prefer the largest output-agreement cluster' — is AlphaCode-C, it has been measured since 2022, and at n=100 on a 6.7B model it is worth +1.3pp on HumanEval and +5.4pp on MBPP, and is NEGATIVE on 2 of 4 model-benchmark cells. CodeT states clustering is 'consistently inferior on both HumanEval and MBPP' and diagnoses why: clustering alone is captured by trivial incorrect solutions that all agree (e.g. all return None / all crash identically). Our regime makes this worse, not better, because a 3B q4_k_m receiver at k<=8 will produce degenerate agreement clusters at a higher rate than InCoder-6B at n=100. Actionable: do NOT run plain agreement clustering as the headline arm. The DOCE result (H2) is the one that works, and the difference between them is (a) the visible-test filter applied FIRST, which kills the trivial-agreement cluster, and (b) Bayes-risk scoring rather than raw cluster size. So our arm must be Filter-then-MBR, i.e. restrict to candidates passing the one visible MBPP assertion, then take the largest execution-agreement cluster among survivors. That is the only version with sub-8B evidence behind it.

title: Semantic Voting: Execution-Grounded Consensus for LLM Code Generation
venue_date: arXiv:2605.08680, cs.SE, submitted 9 May 2026. Shan Jiang, Zijian Yi, Chenguang Zhu.
what_it_does: The most recent and most direct study of our candidate method on our benchmarks. SemanticVote clusters candidates by 'execution fingerprints on LLM-generated inputs' — i.e. execution agreement with SELF-GENERATED inputs, which is precisely the variant we would have to build given our visible/hidden split. 18 configurations across models and thinking levels, with a factorial ablation over input-generation strategy and aggregation rule.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER. Benchmarks HumanEval+ (164 problems) and MBPP+ (378 problems). N=50 candidates standard, N=100 ablation. Greedy single-sample baseline 76.2-95.7% on HumanEval+ and 91.3-96.6% on MBPP+. Best execution-based selector 92.1-98.8% on HumanEval+ and 90.7-97.4% on MBPP+. Output-pattern majority voting 43.9-77.4%, i.e. 19-52 percentage points BELOW the best execution-based selector on every one of the 18 configurations, and below plain greedy decoding. Oracle pass@k on HumanEval+ ~93.9% (Flash Lite) to ~99% (Pro). Residual selection failures average 1.5-2.7% across configurations, with generation failures dominating the remainder. Input-generation ablation: sketch-based input generation beats direct LLM generation by 0.6-2.1 pp and beats random fuzzing by up to 11.3 pp; the paper's own verdict is that 'input quality' is the largest single factor. Aggregation rule barely matters among execution-based methods. Thinking depth helps majority voting by ~12 pp but is flat-to-negative for execution-based methods.
small_k_evidence: NONE. N=50 is the standard configuration, N=100 the ablation, and the paper gives no discussion of smaller candidate budgets in its primary results. NOT REPORTED at k<=8.
small_model_evidence: NONE, and worse than absent — the three receivers are gemini-3.1-pro-preview, gemini-3-flash-preview and gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview, all closed API endpoints with UNDISCLOSED parameter counts. Even flash-lite is very likely far above 8B and is certainly not quantized. Their weakest configuration's greedy baseline is 76.2% on HumanEval+ and 91.3% on MBPP+, i.e. their WEAKEST model is stronger than our 3B's 0.7169 across the combined pool. NOT FOUND for sub-8B.
bearing_on_our_decision: Two things, pulling in opposite directions. Supporting: it confirms execution agreement on self-generated inputs — the version we can actually run — works, and that its residual selection failure is only 1.5-2.7%, which would be an enormous result if it transferred. Also confirms that TEXT-level majority voting is worthless (19-52 pp behind), so we should not waste calls on output-string voting as a comparison arm. Costing us: the 11.3 pp swing between sketch-based and random-fuzzed inputs quantifies the price of not having hidden test inputs, and it is large enough to eat most of the 4.6-5.7 pp we projected from H2. Their input generation itself costs receiver calls, which our 909-calls/hour budget has to absorb on top of 8 draws per task. And this paper is the reason we cannot claim novelty on 'execution agreement for code selection' as a method — our only defensible novelty on this axis is the regime (k<=8, sub-8B, quantized, one visible assertion) plus the causal design. The evidence gap is stark and should be stated in our writeup verbatim: the two 2026 papers that establish this method use N=50-100 candidates and undisclosed-size frontier API models, and neither reports a single number in our operating regime.

title: Optimal Stopping vs Best-of-N for Inference Time Optimization
venue_date: arXiv:2510.01394, cs.LG, submitted 1 October 2025. Yusuf Kalayci, Vinod Raman, Shaddin Dughmi.
what_it_does: Formalizes exactly the second half of our surviving claim — WHEN TO STOP spending inference compute — but as an optimal-stopping/algorithmic-economics problem, not a causal one. Models each LLM generation as opening a costly box with a random reward, i.e. Pandora's Box, and uses Weitzman's algorithm as the known-distribution optimum. Contributes a UCB-style learning algorithm that is 'provably close to Weitzman's algorithm' without knowing the distribution, plus a Bradley-Terry-inspired reward transformation to normalize rewards across prompts and learn stopping thresholds adaptively.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: the adaptive stopping strategy matches Best-of-N quality while using 15-35% fewer generations on average, across multiple LLM/reward-model pairs. Datasets AlpacaFarm and HH-RLHF. NOT FOUND: the specific values of N tested, model names and sizes, and any per-dataset accuracy table are not recoverable from the abstract/landing page; I did not obtain them.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED. No N values are stated in what I could verify.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED. No model names or parameter counts recovered.
bearing_on_our_decision: The stopping half of our claim is occupied methodologically but not causally, and not on our outcome. This paper is the correct citation for 'stopping has a principled optimum' and it gives us the number our stopping arm must beat: 15-35% call reduction at matched quality. But note what it is NOT: reward-model-scored open-ended preference data (AlpacaFarm, HH-RLHF), so the reward is a learned scalar, not a programmatic pass/fail from hidden tests. There is no propensity, no randomization, no off-policy estimator, and no code generation. Our differentiator on stopping is therefore: programmatic binary outcome, known logging propensities so the stopping rule's value is identified rather than just empirically compared, and a regime where the total budget is 8, not large enough for a UCB threshold-learning argument to be meaningful. That last point cuts both ways — at k<=8 a Weitzman-style threshold rule has very little room to be clever, and our own measured adaptive best-of-N (draw until the visible assertion passes) is already close to the degenerate optimum. We should expect our stopping contribution to be about INFERENCE on the rule's value, not about beating this algorithm.

title: Fixed-Horizon Self-Normalized Inference for Adaptive Experiments via Martingale AIPW/DML with Logged Propensities
venue_date: arXiv:2602.15559, stat.ME / econ.EM / math.ST / stat.ML, submitted 17 February 2026, 32 pages. Gabriel Saco.
what_it_does: This is the statistical engine our design needs, published in the statistics literature with zero LLM contact. Assumes exactly our proposed data-generating process: 'the platform logs the executed randomization probability for each unit' and 'the nuisance regressions used to score unit t are constructed predictably from past data only'. Under no interference, sequential randomization, i.i.d. arrivals and executed overlap on a prespecified scored set, it proves the Studentized AIPW/DML statistic with variance estimated by realized quadratic variation is asymptotically N(0,1) at the PRESPECIFIED HORIZON, without variance stabilization. Simulations show when standard fixed-variance Wald reporting fails.
key_numbers: NOT FOUND for any applied numbers — the abstract states 'Simulations validate the theory and highlight when standard fixed-variance Wald reporting fails' but reports no sample sizes or effect magnitudes I could verify. No LLM or inference-time application is mentioned anywhere in the paper.
small_k_evidence: N/A — not an LLM paper, there is no k. The relevant analogue is that the theory is fixed-horizon, which matches our prespecified 8 draws per task.
small_model_evidence: N/A.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the single most useful methodological citation for our surviving claim, and its existence is the strongest evidence that our niche is OPEN rather than occupied: the exact inference theory for prospectively randomized, propensity-logged sequential decisions was published in February 2026 in stat.ME with no awareness of LLM inference, while the LLM test-time-compute literature (H5, H7, H8, H9) independently built stopping and allocation rules with no propensities and no identification argument. The two halves have not been joined. Concretely for us: it licenses fixed-horizon Wald intervals at our prespecified 8-draw horizon with variance from realized quadratic variation, which is what we want given 230 informative tasks and no ability to run a sequential-monitoring correction. Its conditions are ones we can actually satisfy by construction — we control the randomization and can log the executed probability exactly, and our cross-fitting already fits nuisances on past folds only. The 'no interference' assumption is satisfied trivially per task. This should be the design's inferential backbone rather than anything borrowed from the LLM papers.

title: Adaptive Test-Time Compute Allocation for Reasoning LLMs via Constrained Policy Optimization
venue_date: arXiv:2604.14853, cs.LG, submitted 16 April 2026.
what_it_does: Formalizes budget allocation as maximizing expected accuracy subject to an average compute constraint, then solves it by Lagrangian relaxation that 'decomposes the global constraint into per-instance sub-problems', with a lightweight classifier trained to predict oracle actions from cheap input features. I verified explicitly that it does NOT use causal inference, propensity scores, off-policy evaluation, or randomized compute assignment.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: up to 12.8% RELATIVE accuracy improvement on MATH under matched budget constraints; over 91% imitation accuracy against the oracle allocation. Models DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o-mini, Qwen2.5-7B. Benchmarks MATH and GSM8K. NOT FOUND: absolute pass rates, the budget values, and any per-model breakdown.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED. No candidate budget values recovered.
small_model_evidence: YES, one: Qwen2.5-7B, which is under 8B and is the same family as our 7B receiver. But it is unquantized and evaluated on MATH/GSM8K, not code. Nothing at 3B, nothing quantized.
bearing_on_our_decision: Directly relevant and mildly threatening to one of our stated negative results. Their allocation classifier uses CHEAP INPUT FEATURES and hits >91% imitation of the oracle allocation on MATH/GSM8K — which is superficially in tension with our finding that cheap static features recovered none of the selection gap (fractions -0.18, -0.06, 0.00, 0.00). The reconciliation we should write down, and which is genuinely favourable to us: their features predict PROMPT DIFFICULTY (how much compute to spend on this input), which is a property of the task and is known to be learnable; ours had to predict CANDIDATE CORRECTNESS (which of k near-identical programs passes hidden tests), which is a property of the output. Those are different estimands and their success does not undercut our null. It does, however, tell us where cheap features DO pay off, and that is an argument for putting the allocation/stopping half of our design on cheap task-level features while the selection half uses execution signal. Also note: no propensities, no randomization, no identification — the confirmation that even the April 2026 state of the art in this exact sub-area is decision-theoretic and not causal.

title: Optimal Bayesian Stopping for Efficient Inference of Consistent LLM Answers
venue_date: arXiv:2602.05395, submitted 5 February 2026, revised 31 May 2026. Accepted to ICML 2026.
what_it_does: A Bayesian optimal stopping rule for self-consistency sampling: decide after each draw whether the current answer-count vector justifies stopping. Introduces an 'L-aggregated' policy that tracks only the L-1 most frequent answer counts, with a proof that 'L=3 is all you need' for asymptotic optimality while dominating prior-free baselines. This is the stopping-under-agreement problem in its purest form — the same structure as stopping under execution-cluster agreement, which is what our design would do.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: similar answer accuracy while cutting the number of LLM calls by up to 50%. Theoretical result: L=3 suffices for asymptotic optimality. NOT FOUND: specific benchmarks, model names or sizes, sample budgets, or any accuracy-versus-calls table — the landing page carries none of these and I did not obtain the full text.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED. No k values recovered. Note that the L-aggregation result is about how many answer CLUSTERS to track (L=3), not how many draws.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED. No model sizes recovered.
bearing_on_our_decision: Peer-reviewed at ICML 2026, so this is the stopping-rule baseline a reviewer will ask about, and its 50% call reduction is the bar. Two points in our favour. First, the L=3 theorem is directly transferable and cheap for us: it says a stopping rule that tracks only the top-2 execution-agreement cluster counts is asymptotically as good as tracking the full histogram — at k<=8 with a 3B receiver we will rarely have more than 3 distinct execution fingerprints anyway, so this makes our stopping rule nearly trivial to implement and defensible by citation rather than by our own theory. Second, it is again decision-theoretic with no propensities, no randomization, and no identification claim, and its outcome is answer-consistency, not a hidden-test pass. Combined with H5, the picture is consistent: stopping for LLM inference has been done twice over as optimal stopping and Bayesian decision theory, and zero times as a causally identified sequential regime.

title: Learning How Hard to Think: Input-Adaptive Allocation of LM Computation
venue_date: arXiv:2410.04707, submitted 7 October 2024. Damani et al.
what_it_does: Predicts the distribution of rewards given an input and a computation budget, then allocates extra computation to the inputs where it is predicted to help most. Two instantiations: adaptive best-of-k with a dynamically chosen k feeding a reranker, and routing between an expensive/accurate and a cheap/weaker decoding procedure. Code generation is one of three named application domains alongside numerical reasoning and dialog.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: reduces computation by up to 50% at no cost to response quality, OR improves quality by up to 10% at a fixed computational budget. NOT FOUND: k values, budget grids, model names and sizes, and the per-domain code-generation numbers are not in the abstract and I did not recover them.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED in what I verified.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED in what I verified.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the origin of the '50% compute reduction from adaptive best-of-k' figure that recurs in this literature, and it is the closest prior art to our own measured adaptive best-of-N arm. It establishes that ADAPTIVE k is the right frame and that the gains are in compute saved rather than accuracy gained — which matches our paired result (adaptive BoN beat the multi-turn feedback loop at lower cost, paired difference -0.0182, 95% CI [-0.0260, -0.0105]). Verified absent: causal inference, propensity scores, off-policy evaluation. So our contribution against it is again the identification layer plus the fact that our comparison is prospectively randomized rather than a fixed-policy benchmark sweep. Caveat for honesty in our writeup: we should not present adaptive best-of-N as our idea; it is Damani et al.'s, and our measured 0.0182 is a replication in a much smaller regime with a paired interval, which is a real but modest contribution.

title: Feedback Over Form: Why Execution Feedback Matters More Than Pipeline Topology in 1-3B Code Generation
venue_date: arXiv:2604.21950v1, cs.SE, 23 April 2026.
what_it_does: The ONLY paper I found operating in our actual regime — 1-3B code models, HumanEval and MBPP-sanitized, pass@1 with hidden test assertions, run through Ollama-style local endpoints. Compares linear Generator -> Executor -> [Analyzer] -> Refiner pipelines with 1-3 refinement stages, plus NEAT-evolved topologies, and concludes that execution feedback rather than pipeline structure is the load-bearing mechanism.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, 5-run means +/- sd, reported as PROBLEMS PASSED not rates. HumanEval n=164 (7-10 hidden assertions each), MBPP-sanitized n=427 (3 assertions each). Llama3.2:3B solo 76.6 +/- 3.7 HumanEval, 255.8 +/- 5.5 MBPP. Llama self-refine x3: 94.0 +/- 2.7 and 286.2 +/- 2.9. Qwen1.5B -> Llama3B cross-refine 93.6 +/- 3.0 and 287.0 +/- 2.0. NEAT champion 98.2 +/- 3.4 HumanEval. Qwen2.5-coder:3B solo 133.6 +/- 3.4 and 295.4 +/- 5.4; its self-refine 139.6 +/- 2.5 and 307.2 +/- 4.3. Effect sizes: self-refine vs solo +17.4 problems (4.7 sigma) HumanEval, +30.4 (4.9 sigma) MBPP; cross-model vs self-refine -0.4 (0.1 sigma), null; NEAT champion vs manual baseline +4.2 (1.0 sigma), not significant; coder specialization +45.6 (12.4 sigma). Error-class fix rates: SyntaxError 100%, NameError 50-67%, AssertionError only 4-24%. Without early stopping every refinement iteration is net-negative, -6 to -22 net NEW failures per iteration (Table 4); with early stopping, cumulative passes rise from 69 to 99 over 3 iterations (Table 5). Single-run results inflated by 5-7% versus 5-run means. INFERRED rate conversions: Llama3.2:3B solo 76.6/164 = 46.7% HumanEval and 255.8/427 = 59.9% MBPP; Qwen2.5-coder:3B solo 81.5% and 69.2%; coder self-refine 85.1% and 71.9%.
small_k_evidence: N/A in the best possible way — this paper uses pass@1 single attempt with NO sampling, so k=1. It therefore tells us nothing about selection among draws, but everything about what a 3B receiver's failures look like, which is the input to whether selection can work at all.
small_model_evidence: YES, and it is the only paper in this set squarely in our band: Gemma3:1B, Qwen2.5:1.5B, Llama3.2:3B, and Qwen2.5-coder:3B. Same scale as our Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, same benchmarks, same local-inference setting.
bearing_on_our_decision: The most useful paper for calibrating our own numbers and it corroborates three of our findings independently. (1) Their AssertionError fix rate of 4-24% versus 100% for SyntaxError is the mechanistic explanation for our 0.0737 residual gap: at 3B the surviving failures are LOGIC errors, and logic errors are what neither refinement nor cheap static features can touch. This is the sentence our writeup needs to explain why our GBM recovered nothing. (2) 'Without early stopping every iteration is net-negative, -6 to -22 net new failures per iteration' is direct external support for our paired result that adaptive best-of-N beats a real multi-turn feedback loop, and it locates the mechanism in the absence of a stopping rule rather than in the feedback being useless. That makes STOPPING, not selection, the part of our surviving claim with the clearest external backing. (3) Their 5-7% single-run inflation versus 5-run means is a direct warning about our own audit: any single-pass estimate in our logs is optimistic by roughly that much, which matters because our 7B gap is only 0.0351 and could be substantially noise. We should check whether our 0.7169/0.7455/0.8192 figures are single-run. What it does NOT cover: no candidate selection, no agreement clustering, no k>1, no propensities, no causal framing, and its topology search is evolutionary rather than randomized.

title: Offline Policy Evaluation of Multi-Turn LLM Health Coaching with Real Users
venue_date: arXiv:2510.17173, submitted 20 October 2025, revised 21 October 2025. NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Multi-Turn Interactions in Large Language Models. Melik Ozolcer, Sang Won Bae.
what_it_does: The nearest existing attempt at off-policy evaluation of a MULTI-TURN LLM policy with real users — i.e. the multi-round dynamic-treatment-regime framing our project started from. Uses factorized decision heads over tool use and communication style, and evaluates candidate policies with 'a lightweight simulator with hidden archetypes', i.e. model-based OPE rather than importance weighting.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: seven users, 280 rated conversation turns. Outcomes are 'typed rewards' combining objective tool outcomes with subjective satisfaction ratings. Key finding: a uniform heavy-tool policy improved average performance but HARMED a specific subgroup, low-health-literacy users with high self-efficacy, motivating per-archetype reporting. NOT FOUND: propensity scores, known propensities, or randomization are not mentioned in the abstract; no IPS/DR estimator is named; no effect sizes or confidence intervals recovered.
small_k_evidence: N/A — no candidate sampling. The sequential dimension is conversation turns, not draws.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED.
bearing_on_our_decision: Useful mainly as evidence of how thin the multi-turn-LLM OPE literature actually is. Seven users and 280 turns, evaluated through a simulator with no propensities, at a workshop — that is the state of the art for causal/off-policy evaluation of multi-round LLM policies as of late 2025. Our 230-informative-task design with KNOWN logging propensities and a PROGRAMMATIC binary outcome is quantitatively and methodologically stronger than this on every axis except realism of the interaction. It also flags a real risk for us: their headline result is that an average improvement masked subgroup harm, which for us maps onto the difficulty band — a selection policy that improves the pooled 561-task rate could be net-negative on the easy or the hardest band. We should prespecify band-stratified reporting, which our 230-task informative band already sets up.

title: Micro-Randomized Trials: An Experimental Design for Developing Just-in-Time Adaptive Interventions; and The stratified micro-randomized trial design
venue_date: Klasnja, Hekler, Shiffman, Boruvka, Almirall, Tewari, Murphy, Health Psychology 2015, PMC4732571. Stratified MRT: arXiv:1711.03587 (Dempsey, Liao, Klasnja, Nahum-Shani, Murphy).
what_it_does: The design template our project's framing borrows from. An MRT is a trial with rapid sequential randomizations in which the same unit is randomized to intervention options hundreds or thousands of times, with the explicit purpose of estimating time-varying causal effects of moment-level treatments to build a just-in-time adaptive intervention. The stratified variant handles sample-size calculation for nested causal effects of time-varying treatments.
key_numbers: Design/methodology, not benchmark numbers. Relevant structural facts MEASURED-IN-PAPER: repeated randomization of the same unit hundreds-to-thousands of times is the design's premise; the stratified paper's contribution is sample-size formulas for testing nested time-varying causal effects. Also confirmed in this literature: the multi-step setting breaks plain IPW because sequential propensities compound and variance grows exponentially in the number of time steps. NOT FOUND: no LLM or inference-time application in either paper.
small_k_evidence: N/A for candidates, but structurally adverse: MRTs assume MANY randomization occasions per unit. Our per-task horizon is 8, which is 2-3 orders of magnitude below the regime these designs are powered for.
small_model_evidence: N/A.
bearing_on_our_decision: Two consequences, one enabling and one limiting. Enabling: the MRT literature is the right citation for why a prospectively randomized sequential design is the correct instrument here, and the framing 'each draw-or-stop decision is a micro-randomization occasion' is legitimate and unoccupied in the LLM setting. Limiting, and this is the number that matters: MRT power is built on hundreds-to-thousands of occasions per unit, and we have at most 8, with 230 informative tasks. Our power therefore comes almost entirely from the CROSS-TASK dimension, not the within-task sequential dimension, which means we should be honest that our design is closer to a stratified 8-occasion micro-randomized trial than to a mobile-health MRT, and that any claim about the time-varying structure of the effect across draw index 1 through 8 will be badly underpowered. The compounding-variance warning about sequential IPW is also a direct instruction to use the AIPW/DML form from H6 rather than plain importance weighting.

title: Scaling LLM Inference with Optimized Sample Compute Allocation (OSCA)
venue_date: arXiv:2410.22480, 29 October 2024. NAACL 2025 (aclanthology 2025.naacl-long.404).
what_it_does: Hill-climbing search for an optimal MIXED allocation of a fixed sample budget across inference configurations (model, temperature, language, prompt) rather than picking a single configuration. Relevant to us as the strongest published demonstration that allocation alone, with no better selector, buys large compute multiples — and as the one allocation paper that reports small budgets.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: on LiveCodeBench with only 8 samples, OSCA's pass rate reaches 67%, exceeding the pass rate of the default pure allocation at 128 samples — a 128x compute reduction. On SWE-Bench, 3x less compute than the default configuration. Budgets swept from 2 through 512-1024 samples, so 4, 8 and 16 are included. Benchmarks LiveCodeBench, LiveBench, SWE-Bench Lite. Models GPT-4o, Llama3-70B, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen2-70B.
small_k_evidence: YES, and it is the best small-budget evidence in this set: an explicit headline result AT 8 SAMPLES, which is exactly our planned k. The 67%-at-8-samples versus default-at-128 comparison is the cleanest published demonstration that decisions made at k=8 can be worth two orders of magnitude of naive compute.
small_model_evidence: NONE. Every model is a frontier API or a 70B open model. The smallest is Llama3-70B / Qwen2-70B, roughly 10x our 7B and 23x our 3B, and none are quantized. NOT FOUND for sub-8B.
bearing_on_our_decision: The most encouraging small-k datapoint available, with the caveat that it is at the wrong model scale and optimizes a different lever. What transfers: k=8 is not a hopeless budget — OSCA gets a 128x compute multiple out of decisions made at exactly 8 samples, which is a direct rebuttal to the objection that our k<=8 regime is too small for any selection or allocation policy to matter. What does not transfer: OSCA allocates across CONFIGURATIONS, and we have one receiver at one temperature, so the lever it pulls is unavailable to us. Also, its gains come from diversity across configurations, which is precisely the mechanism a single quantized 3B at fixed temperature lacks — and low candidate diversity is exactly what makes execution-agreement clusters degenerate (see H3). This is worth testing directly and cheaply: if our 8 draws produce fewer than 3 distinct execution fingerprints on most tasks, agreement clustering cannot possibly recover 0.0737, and that diagnostic costs zero receiver calls because our existing 3-4-draw logs already contain it.

title: Selection Without Signal, Recovery Through Expression: A Measurement Study of Post-Hoc Falsification Operators for Frozen Small Code Models
venue_date: arXiv:2606.16999v1, cs.SE, submitted 15 June 2026, preprint (single author, Mehmet Iscan, PythaLab / Yildiz Technical University). NOT peer-reviewed.
what_it_does: Exactly our experiment, one notch smaller. Takes FROZEN small code models, samples k=8 candidates per task at T=0.8 with SHA256-seeded reproducibility, and tests 26 post-hoc operators (selection / verification / repair / elimination / generation-conditioning / compute-allocation) against a matched-compute Best-of-N baseline under a leakage-free visible/hidden split, with a do-no-harm bar (McNemar b10=0) and distribution-free certificates. Explicitly includes execution-consensus (MBR-Exec-style fingerprint plurality) as operator family #1, and an adaptive consensus early-STOP rule (ACE) as the compute-allocation operator. Benchmarks: HumanEval+ (164), MBPP+ (370 after a determinism gate dropped 8/378), plus two self-authored suites.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: k=8; models DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B, Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B, Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, served locally via Ollama. DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B on HumanEval+: standard extraction 29/164, BoN(8) 29/164, oracle 29/164 -- an 'empty consensus trap', i.e. ZERO selector-agnostic headroom. Selector-agnostic ceiling (oracle minus BoN) = 0 tasks on the DeepSeek cell, 6-7 tasks on the two Qwen cells. Realized leakage-free consensus gain = 0-2 tasks, never significant (p >= 0.25). 'Capability scissors': among visible-passing candidates, residual hidden-correctness signal is at chance -- AUC 0.479 on Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B, 0.483 for embeddings alone. Verdict on the whole semantic output space: 'every operator ... is null, negative, or falsified.' Coverage wall: at k=16 on a held-out hard set, 16/30 tasks still produce NO hidden-correct candidate. Only two wins, both outside output-space selection: M1 expression-layer recovery (HumanEval+ 29->41, +12 tasks, p=2.4e-4, b10=0; MBPP+ 128->161, +33 tasks, p=1.2e-10, b10=0) and ACE early-stop (~19% receiver-call reduction at zero harm, Hoeffding-Bentkus p=0.0165; 63.9% reduction at tau=1 but b10=2 tasks harmed). Proposition 1: distribution-free certificates need n >= 45 tasks.
small_k_evidence: MEASURED-IN-PAPER at exactly k=8, the planned k of our design. This is the ONLY paper found that runs the selection question at our k on small local models. It says: at k=8 the headroom is 0-7 tasks and consensus recovers 0-2 of them, p >= 0.25.
small_model_evidence: MEASURED-IN-PAPER for 0.5B / 1.3B / 1.5B -- all BELOW our 3B and 7B. No 3B, no 7B, no quantized (q4_k_m) cell, no Qwen2.5-Instruct (only Qwen2.5-Coder). Served by Ollama, not llama.cpp directly.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the paper that gets us rejected. It pre-empts BOTH halves of the narrowed contribution: (a) the negative result that cheap post-hoc selection cannot recover the gap, including cross-candidate execution agreement, with a stronger experimental protocol than ours (26 operators, do-no-harm bar, leakage gate, determinism gate); and (b) the stopping rule, with a certified 19%-compute-saving adaptive consensus early-stop. Its AUC 0.479 for residual hidden-correctness among visible-passers is the precise mechanism our own gradient-boosted and logistic nulls observed, already named and explained ('capability scissors', 'consensus trap', 'coverage wall'). The only defensible wedge left: it stops at 1.5B unquantized and never tests 3B/7B, never tests quantization, is single-author and unreviewed, and its DeepSeek cell has literally zero oracle headroom (29=29=29), which means its headline null is partly a pool problem, not a selector problem. Our 3B has a real 0.0737 residual gap above the visible-verdict rule -- an order of magnitude more headroom than their 0-task cell. Cite it, replicate ACE as a BASELINE, and position at 3B-7B quantized where it is silent.

title: Inference-Time Code Selection via Symbolic Equivalence Partitioning (SEP)
venue_date: arXiv:2604.06485v2, 13 May 2026, preprint (Cho, Wang, Sui, Grama -- Purdue / Texas Instruments)
what_it_does: Precisely the 'obvious untested candidate' we named, in its strongest form. First filters candidates by the problem's PUBLIC examples (exactly our visible-assertion rule), then uses bounded symbolic execution (CrossHair) to partition survivors into functional-equivalence classes and returns the representative of the largest class. Requires no auxiliary test generation, no learned verifier, no extra LLM inference. Evaluated at N in {5,10,20} on HumanEval+ (164) and a 438-problem filtered LiveCodeBench, against Pass@1, CodeBLEU consensus, embedding consensus, LLM-as-judge, CodeT, SRank, with Pass@N as the oracle ceiling.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, HumanEval+ N=10, seven models 4B-20B: average Pass@1 0.754 -> SEP 0.826, average Pass@10 0.8729. Per model (Pass@1 / CodeT / SRank / SEP / Pass@10): Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 0.589/0.635/0.657/0.689/0.787; Phi-4-mini-instruct 0.647/0.724/0.730/0.793/0.854; Qwen3-4B 0.749/0.786/0.792/0.799/0.835; Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 0.804/0.809/0.821/0.829/0.860; Qwen3-14B 0.845/0.868/0.862/0.878/0.896; Phi-4-reasoning 0.826/0.863/0.865/0.902/0.927; gpt-oss-20b 0.820/0.864/0.858/0.890/0.951. MEASURED-IN-PAPER, HumanEval+ N=5: average Pass@1 0.7547, CodeT 0.7853, SRank 0.7876, SEP 0.8083, Pass@5 0.8527. INFERRED (my arithmetic on their tables) -- fraction of the Pass@1-to-Pass@N oracle gap closed: at N=10, mean gap 0.1186, CodeT closes 32.4%, SRank 36.7%, SEP 60.2%; at N=5, mean gap 0.0980, CodeT closes 31.2%, SRank 33.5%, SEP 54.7%. INFERRED for the three sub-5B cells only (Phi-4-mini 3.8B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-4B-Instruct) at N=5: mean gap 0.0993, CodeT closes 30.5%, SEP closes 53.0%. Also MEASURED-IN-PAPER: pairwise symbolic-equivalence accuracy mean 0.884 over 42 model-budget settings (0.900 HumanEval+); partition failures on consensus-eligible instances 505/8969 = 5.63%; SEP wall-clock 539s (N=5) to 2723s (N=10-20) on HumanEval+ versus CodeT's 11192s of auxiliary test generation.
small_k_evidence: MEASURED-IN-PAPER at N=5 and N=10 -- inside our regime. The paper states SEP 'is already effective at N=5, making it practical even under tight candidate budgets.' Full N=5 tables are in Appendix A (their Tables 3 and 5).
small_model_evidence: MEASURED-IN-PAPER for Phi-4-mini-instruct (~3.8B), Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct -- i.e. models bracketing our 3B and 7B. NOT REPORTED: any quantized model, any Qwen2.5-Instruct, and any MBPP/MBPP-sanitized result (HumanEval+ and LiveCodeBench only).
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the direct answer to our viability question, and it answers YES: a cheap method that never sees hidden tests recovers about half the oracle gap at k=5-10 on 4B-8B open models. Our 3B gap of 0.1023 (0.7169 -> 0.8192) is statistically indistinguishable in magnitude from their mean N=5 gap of 0.0980, so the literature predicts agreement/equivalence clustering should buy us roughly 0.031 (CodeT-strength) to 0.055 (SEP-strength) absolute on the 3B. That is 4-7x our measured 0.0182 adaptive-BoN-vs-feedback effect, so it is worth the compute. The reviewer's kill shot, though, is that SEP's headline improvement is measured against raw Pass@1, NOT against public-test filtering -- and public filtering is SEP's own first stage. Our visible-assertion rule already closes 28.0% of our gap (INFERRED: (0.7455-0.7169)/0.1023), which is almost exactly the whole of CodeT's 31.2%. So the honest quantity is SEP-minus-public-filter, which this paper never isolates. That missing number is our only real opening, and H4 suggests it may be near zero at 7B.

title: Semantic Voting: Execution-Grounded Consensus for LLM Code Generation
venue_date: arXiv:2605.08680v1, 12 May 2026, preprint (Jiang, Yi, Zhu -- UT Austin). Self-described 'findings paper'.
what_it_does: Isolates the exact axis we proposed to study: how much does the AGGREGATION RULE matter once candidates are executed on common inputs? Clusters candidates by execution fingerprints on LLM-generated inputs (SemanticVote) and compares against output-pattern majority voting, weighted voting and MBR-Exec across 18 configurations (3 Gemini models x 3 thinking levels x HumanEval+ / MBPP+), with paired bootstrap tests (10,000 problem-level resamples) and a formal oracle-gap decomposition into generation failures vs selection failures.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, oracle-gap decomposition (their Table 5): selection failures average 1.8% (SemanticVote) and 1.5% (weighted voting) across the 9 HumanEval+ configs, and 2.7% / 2.5% across the 9 MBPP+ configs; generation failures average 2.8% and 3.9%. On Gemini 3.1 Pro low, oracle 98.8 = SV 98.8 = WV 98.8, selection failure rate 0.0% -- the selection gap is closed COMPLETELY. Flash medium: oracle 98.8, SV 96.3, WV 96.3, selection failure 2.4%. Lite low: oracle 93.9, SV 92.1, WV 92.7, selection failure 1.8% / 1.2%. MEASURED-IN-PAPER, aggregation rule is irrelevant: SV-minus-WV lies in [-0.79, +0.61] pp and SV-minus-MBR-Exec in [-0.61, +1.22] pp, with p > 0.05 on ALL 18 configurations. Execution-based selectors beat output-pattern majority voting by 19-52 pp (MV scores 43.9-77.4% on HumanEval+, 39.4-77.2% on MBPP+). AST-normalized MV recovers 20-40 pp of that but still trails by 1.8-3.1 pp. Input quality dominates: sketch-based input generation beats direct LLM inputs by 0.6-2.1 pp and beats random fuzzing or example-only inputs by up to 11.3 pp. D-scaling (number of common inputs): pass@1 95.1 at D=5, 96.3 at D=10, saturates at 97.0 for D>=30; average largest cluster holds 47-48 of 50 candidates. Notable inversion: on Flash medium/high, plain GREEDY decoding (95.2 on MBPP+) BEATS every execution-based selector (91.0-92.3).
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED. N=50 throughout, N=100 for the input-strategy ablation. The only budget they scale is D (number of common inputs, 5 to 50), not the number of candidates. No k <= 10 anywhere.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED, and this is the paper's own stated limitation. Only three frontier proprietary endpoints: gemini-3.1-pro-preview, gemini-3-flash-preview, gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview. Nothing open-weight, nothing under 8B, nothing quantized.
bearing_on_our_decision: Two-edged, and both edges cut us. First edge: a reviewer will say the selection gap is ALREADY CLOSED -- selection failures of 1.5-2.7% and one config at exactly 0.0% mean there is nothing left for a causally-framed policy to recover, so our headroom is uninteresting. Second edge, more damaging to our specific plan: the aggregation RULE does not matter (p > 0.05 in 18/18); what matters is the quality of the common inputs. Any contribution we frame as a better agreement/stopping rule is pre-refuted; the live variable is input synthesis, which for us means asking a 3B q4_k_m model to generate discriminating inputs -- and the paper notes the all-success filter fails hardest 'on weaker models, where more generated candidates hit at least one generated-input error.' The exploitable gap is stark and we should say it out loud: every number here comes from Gemini 3.x frontier models at N=50 on benchmarks with ~35x augmented test suites. It is silent at k<=8 and below 8B, and the Flash-medium inversion (greedy 95.2 beats selection 91.0-92.3) is direct evidence that selection can HURT when per-candidate quality is low -- which is our regime.

title: S*: Test Time Scaling for Code Generation
venue_date: arXiv:2502.14382v1, 20 Feb 2025; published as Findings of EMNLP 2025 (aclanthology.org/2025.findings-emnlp.865). Li, Cao, Cao, Li, Tan, Keutzer, Xing, Gonzalez, Stoica -- UC Berkeley.
what_it_does: Hybrid parallel + sequential test-time scaling for code, whose Stage 2 is a selection mechanism: prompt an LLM to synthesize inputs that DISTINGUISH paired candidates, execute both on them, and let execution results decide. Evaluated across 12 models including the full Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct ladder (0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, 14B, 32B) on LiveCodeBench v2 (511 problems) and CodeContests (165). Config: 16 parallel samples at T=0.7, 2 rounds of debugging. Contains the single most decision-relevant ablation I found anywhere in this literature: Table 3, a head-to-head of four selection policies at N=8.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, Table 3, LiveCodeBench v4, N=8, T=0.7, four selection policies (Public-tests-only / Generated-tests / LLM-judge / Adaptive-input-synthesis): Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct 42.3 / 42.3 / 42.3 / 44.5; Qwen2.5-Coder-32B 54.6 / 57.8 / 55.5 / 58.3; GPT-4o-mini 54.1 / 55.2 / 56.3 / 57.3; QwQ-32B-Preview 64.3 / 65.9 / 68.6 / 69.7; average 53.8 / 53.1 / 55.6 / 57.5. INFERRED: on the 7B at N=8, generated-test agreement buys +0.0 pp over public-test filtering and the cleverest available selector buys +2.2 pp; averaged over all four models, generated-test agreement is NEGATIVE at -0.7 pp versus public-only. MEASURED-IN-PAPER, Table 1, LiveCodeBench v2 pass@1 for Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct at 0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B: zero-shot 1.2/7.0/18.4/29.4; majority vote (execution clustering, N=16, AlphaCode-style) 2.5/11.0/25.2/40.5; self-debugging 2.4/9.4/27.8/39.9; S* 10.9/27.6/42.7/54.4. MEASURED-IN-PAPER, CodeContests: Qwen-Coder-7B zero-shot 1.8 -> S* 10.9 -> S*(Oracle) 12.1. MEASURED-IN-PAPER: at N=1 Qwen2.5-Coder-7B is the weakest model yet gains the most from repeated sampling (>35% at N=64) -- but also 'exhibits performance regression at higher temperatures.' Important caveat the paper states plainly: GPT-4o-mini generates the inputs for the majority-voting clustering and refines code for reasoning models -- the selection signal for the small models is manufactured by a much larger model.
small_k_evidence: MEASURED-IN-PAPER at N=8 for the selection-policy ablation (Table 3) -- the closest published match to our planned k=8. Also N in {1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128} for coverage curves (Figure 4), though those are pass@N not selected-pass@1.
small_model_evidence: MEASURED-IN-PAPER for Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B and 7B -- the same family and the same two sizes as our receivers, though Coder rather than plain Instruct, and unquantized. NOT REPORTED: MBPP or HumanEval (LiveCodeBench v2/v4 and CodeContests only), and no quantized inference.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the most useful hit in the whole set, and it is bad news dressed as good news. It is the only paper that reports our exact contrast -- 'select among candidates that pass the visible tests' versus 'select using cross-candidate execution evidence' -- at our exact k on a 7B Qwen2.5. The answer at 7B, N=8 is +0.0 pp, and the four-model average for generated-test agreement is -0.7 pp. That is a direct prediction that cross-candidate execution agreement will recover NONE of our 7B residual gap of 0.0351, and it converges with H1's AUC 0.479. The +2.2 pp that S*'s adaptive input synthesis does buy at 7B requires an LLM to synthesize discriminating inputs per candidate pair -- at 909 receiver calls per hour, pairwise input synthesis over 8 candidates on 230 tasks is thousands of extra calls, and in the paper that synthesis was done by GPT-4o-mini, not by the small receiver. Also note their 16-sample majority-vote row (execution clustering) does lift the 3B from 18.4 to 25.2 and the 7B from 29.4 to 40.5, but that is measured from zero-shot, not from a visible-test-filtered baseline, so it is not comparable to our 0.7455.

title: Inference Scaling fLaws / The Limits of Inference Scaling Through Resampling
venue_date: arXiv:2411.17501, v1 26 Nov 2024, v3 26 Mar 2026 (Stroebl, Kapoor, Narayanan -- Princeton CITP). Widely cited; the arXiv listing I read does not name a peer-reviewed venue.
what_it_does: Attacks the validity of the oracle-gap framing itself. Shows that resampling-based inference scaling is bounded by the FALSE POSITIVE rate of the verifier -- solutions that pass the visible/available tests but are actually wrong. Because resampling cannot reduce the false-positive probability, there is a hard ceiling on achievable accuracy independent of compute. Establishes the ceiling on HumanEval and MBPP specifically, the two benchmarks whose unit tests have known limited coverage, and then does a cost-benefit analysis of the optimal number of samples.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: false-positive rate is strongly and inversely linearly correlated with single-sample accuracy across model families (Llama-3.1 8B and 70B, Code Llama 7B and 13B, GPT-4o, Cohere Command, Phi-3) on HumanEval+; weaker models produce false positives at substantially higher rates. Core result: models below a performance threshold 'cannot match the performance of a single invocation of a stronger model, no matter how big the compute budget.' Cost-benefit result: even with zero compute cost, the optimal number of attempts is 'finite and very low (e.g. K <= 5)'; at a 4:1 false-positive-cost to correct-solution-benefit ratio, optimal K <= 5 for ALL tested models; at 10:1, the optimal number of samples is K = 0. Conclusion as stated: weaker models cannot 'sample their way' to top-level performance when verifiers have imperfect coverage.
small_k_evidence: MEASURED-IN-PAPER and in our favour on the compute question: the paper's own conclusion is that optimal K is 5 or below under realistic false-positive costs, which independently justifies our k<=8 design against the k=50-1000 convention. But it reaches that conclusion by arguing the gap is not worth chasing, not that it is recoverable.
small_model_evidence: MEASURED-IN-PAPER for Llama-3.1-8B, Code Llama 7B and 13B, Phi-3 variants -- the 7B-8B band. NOT REPORTED for 3B or below, and no quantized models.
bearing_on_our_decision: The reviewer uses this to attack our headline number. Our ORACLE pass@3 of 0.8192 is defined by our own hidden tests; to the extent those hidden tests are incomplete, part of the 0.0737 residual gap is false-positive headroom that no selector should recover and that we would be rewarded for chasing. This paper documents exactly that failure mode on HumanEval and MBPP, and shows the effect is WORSE for weaker models -- and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct at q4_k_m is squarely in the weakest band they consider. Two concrete consequences. First, we must report the false-positive rate of our own visible-assertion selector against hidden tests as a first-class number, or the whole gap is contestable; our strict one-visible-assertion split is a partial defence but it cuts both ways, since one assertion is a very weak verifier. Second, the paper's K<=5 result is quotable ammunition for our small-k design and against the k=50-1000 literature -- this is the one place where the adversarial literature actually helps us.

title: Optimal Stopping vs Best-of-N for Inference Time Optimization
venue_date: arXiv:2510.01394, submitted 1 Oct 2025, cs.LG / cs.CL; under review at OpenReview (forum fZJvPuadUT). Kalayci et al.
what_it_does: Directly claims the stopping half of our contribution. Frames each generation as opening a costly box whose payoff is a reward-model score, and applies a UCB-style Pandora's Box algorithm (provably close to Weitzman's optimal policy when the distribution is known), plus a Bradley-Terry-inspired transformation to normalize reward scales across prompts and learn stopping thresholds on the fly.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: the adaptive stopping policy matches non-adaptive Best-of-N performance while requiring 15-35% fewer generations on average; win rate over non-adaptive Best-of-N exceeds 54% across most cost settings. Evaluated on multiple LLM-reward-model pairs on AlpacaFarm and HH-RLHF. Compare with H1's ACE early-stop, which achieves ~19% receiver-call reduction at zero harm with a certified Hoeffding-Bentkus p=0.0165 on code at k=8.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED. The abstract and the accessible text give no N sweep and no small-N regime.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED. No model sizes are identified; the setup is 'multiple LLM-reward model pairs', and it REQUIRES a reward model, which we do not have and cannot afford to train on 909 calls/hour.
bearing_on_our_decision: Establishes that 'when to stop spending compute' is a solved problem with a named optimal-stopping pedigree and a 15-35% savings number, so framing stopping as our novelty invites rejection. The defence is narrow but real: this method needs a learned reward model and is validated on open-ended alignment benchmarks (AlpacaFarm, HH-RLHF), not on code with an executable signal, and it never touches sub-8B or quantized receivers. Our stopping rule keys on an execution verdict, not a reward score, which is a genuinely different information structure -- but H1's ACE already occupies even that niche on code at k=8. Realistic posture: treat BOTH as baselines and claim only the causal/randomized estimation of the stopping policy's effect, not the policy.

title: The Larger the Better? Improved LLM Code-Generation via Budget Reallocation
venue_date: Published at COLM 2024; arXiv:2404.00725v2, 25 Jul 2024. Hassid, Remez, Gehring, Schwartz, Adi -- FAIR at Meta / Hebrew University.
what_it_does: Compares running a large model once against a smaller model many times under matched FLOPs and matched wall-clock, on HumanEval, MBPP and three APPS splits, for Code Llama 7B/13B/34B/70B and Llama-3 8B/70B. Then removes the unit-test oracle and asks whether any cheap ranking policy can substitute for it, using averaged negative log-likelihood from rankers of every size plus the released LEVER verifier, scored with a purpose-built rank-score@k estimator. Releases 2,000 Code Llama 7B generations per HumanEval and MBPP task (1,328,000 generations).
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: with unit tests available, repeated use of smaller models yields gains of up to 15% across five tasks, and the 13B model is best across almost all budgets with a consistent 5% margin on the hardest APPS competition split. Without unit tests: NLL-based ranking improves with both budget and ranker size, and a 7B ranking itself beats its own greedy decoding, but ranking multiple generations from a smaller model consistently FAILS to match greedy decoding from a larger model at matched wall-clock (their Figures 8 and 9, rank-score-time@t over normalized wall-time 1 to 16). The LEVER verifier 'does not improve the results in the test-less setting' -- explicitly because its execution-pruning and execution-result components are unavailable without tests. Stated conclusion: 'there remains a gap to bridge between using LLMs as rankers for smaller models and using them as generators.'
small_k_evidence: MEASURED-IN-PAPER over normalized wall-time budgets of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 (which at matched wall-clock corresponds to roughly k=1 to k=16 for the 7B), so the small-budget end of their curves is in our regime. Exact per-k tabulated values are in the figures, not in a table.
small_model_evidence: MEASURED-IN-PAPER for Code Llama 7B and 13B and Llama-3 8B -- the 7B-8B band, unquantized. NOT REPORTED for 3B or below.
bearing_on_our_decision: Supports our measured nulls and simultaneously drains them of novelty. Our finding that cross-fitted gradient boosting and logistic regression over cheap static features recover NONE of the gap (fractions -0.18, -0.06, 0.00, 0.00, all intervals covering zero) is the same phenomenon this COLM 2024 paper established for NLL ranking and for LEVER-without-execution two years earlier, on the same two benchmarks, at the same model scale. A reviewer will say our null is a replication, not a result. The useful reading for us is mechanistic: what fails is every signal that does NOT execute the candidate; what works is execution. That is precisely the argument for testing cross-candidate execution agreement rather than more static features -- and it is why H2's 54.7% at N=5 and H4's +0.0 pp at 7B/N=8 are the two numbers our decision actually turns on. Their released 1.3M generations are also a free, zero-compute way to pre-test an agreement selector at k<=8 on HumanEval and MBPP before spending any of our 909 calls/hour.

title: DOCE: Finding the Sweet Spot for Execution-Based Code Generation
venue_date: arXiv:2408.13745, 25 Aug 2024 (preprint; deep-spin/doce)
what_it_does: The single closest prior work to our exact design. Systematically compares, on one fixed candidate pool: greedy, random, execution-FREE rerankers (log-likelihood LL, Coder-Reviewer CR, and the TRAINED neural metric CodeScore CS), filtering by the visible/trial unit tests, MBR-Exec (cross-candidate output-agreement clustering), their combination, and the oracle. Benchmarks are HumanEval(+) and MBPP-S(+) under EvalPlus hidden tests -- i.e. our benchmark pair and our visible/hidden split.
key_numbers: DeepSeekCoder-6.7B-Instruct, n=50, temp 1.2, EvalPlus (+) numbers, all MEASURED-IN-PAPER (Table 4). HumanEval+: Random 65.1, Greedy 76.8, LL 71.8, CR 70.3, CodeScore 63.6, Filter 78.7, Filter+LL 79.1, Filter+CR 79.6, Filter+CodeScore 78.4, MBR-Exec 85.5, Filter+MBR-Exec 90.7, Oracle 93.2. MBPP-S+: Random 58.6, Greedy 64.3, LL 58.9, CR 64.0, Filter 72.6, Filter+LL 72.8, Filter+CR 72.8, MBR-Exec 78.6, Filter+MBR-Exec 82.1, Oracle 85.6. CodeLlama-7B-Instruct n=50: HumanEval+ / MBPP-S+ Greedy 43.3/53.2, Random 34.1/50.1, Filter 70.0/77.4, MBR-Exec 52.1/64.0, Filter+MBR-Exec 74.5/79.0, Oracle 82.4/83.2 (MEASURED-IN-PAPER). INFERRED from those rows -- fraction of the POST-FILTER oracle gap closed by adding execution agreement: DeepSeek-6.7B 12.0/14.5 = 82.8% on HumanEval+ and 9.5/13.0 = 73.1% on MBPP-S+; CodeLlama-7B 4.5/12.4 = 36.3% and 1.6/5.8 = 27.6%. INFERRED for the execution-free rerankers on top of filtering: LL closes 2.8% (HE+) / 1.5% (MBPP-S+), CR 6.2% / 1.5%, CodeScore -2.1% / NOT REPORTED. Paper's own words: CodeScore "does not even outperform the random baseline".
small_k_evidence: Figure 3 sweeps n in {1,5,10,20,25,50} for CodeLlama-7B-Instruct. Values read off the figure (approximate, figure-only, the paper prints no table): HumanEval+ at n=5 MBR-Exec ~47, Filter ~65, Filter+MBR-Exec ~68; at n=10 ~50 / ~68 / ~71. MBPP-S+ at n=5 ~59 / ~72 / ~73; at n=10 ~61 / ~73 / ~75. So the INCREMENT of execution agreement over visible-test filtering at k=5-10 is only about +1 to +3 points, versus +4.5 to +12.0 at n=50. This is the only small-k, sub-8B, MBPP+HumanEval curve I found anywhere in the literature.
small_model_evidence: Yes, and it is the best match available: DeepSeekCoder-6.7B-Instruct and CodeLlama-7B-Instruct (plus CodeLlama-13B). No 3B model. All unquantized.
bearing_on_our_decision: This paper does two opposite things to us. (1) It CORROBORATES our null precisely: execution-free rerankers stacked on visible-test filtering add +0.2 to +0.9 points (1.5-6.2% of the post-filter gap) on a 6.7B model, and a TRAINED execution-free scorer (CodeScore) is worse than random and worse than filtering alone -- that is our cross-fitted GBM/logistic result, already published, on our benchmarks, at our model scale. Stop spending compute on static-feature learned selectors; cite this. (2) It KILLS any claim that the selection gap is unrecoverable: cross-candidate execution agreement on top of filtering closes 73-83% of the post-filter oracle gap at n=50. CRITICAL CAVEAT that decides how much of that transfers to us: DOCE's MBR-Exec executes candidates on ALL evaluation unit-test INPUTS ("we use all unit tests given but only their inputs"), and the paper states 80% of trial tests overlap the evaluation tests. Our strict split gives exactly ONE visible MBPP assertion, so we must SYNTHESISE the common inputs. DOCE therefore gives an upper bound, not our expected value. Combined with its own n=5/n=10 curve, the honest prediction for us at k=8 is +0.02 to +0.03 pass@1, i.e. 27-41% of our 0.0737 (3B) post-filter gap -- not 73-83%.

title: Oracle Gap and Signal Fidelity: A Fixed-Pool Diagnostic for Test-Time Collaboration
venue_date: arXiv:2607.17531, 20 Jul 2026 (preprint)
what_it_does: Builds the exact decomposition our project needs: net gain of any selector = recoverable mass (oracle gap) x signal coverage x conditional selection quality - harm to already-correct outputs. Applies it at a FIXED pool of k=5 to LiveCodeBench (1,055 tasks), MATH L5, GPQA-Diamond, HumanEval+ as a saturation anchor. Compares a public-test verifier (= our visible-assertion filter), a generated-test verifier, and LLM selectors (same-family L1, cross-model L3).
key_numbers: All MEASURED-IN-PAPER, k=5, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B primary. LiveCodeBench: oracle gap 11.74pp (339/2,888 recoverable). Public-test verifier +8.14pp, MCC 0.825, coverage 85.66% of rows, 0% harm, captures 69% of recoverable cases. Generated-test verifier +2.70pp, MCC 0.248, coverage only 35.77%, 0.10% harm, captures 23% of recoverable cases. LLM selector L1 +3.50pp with 4.69% harm rate; L3 +1.97pp with 5.65% harm; L1 is NOT statistically distinguishable from the generated-test verifier. MATH L5: symbolic-equivalence agreement +4.67pp over self-consistency (39 fixed / 4 harmed), while the L1 LLM selector is -3.20pp. GPQA-Diamond: oracle gap only 3.03pp, L1 selector -1.68pp, 5/18 captured vs 15/283 harmed. HumanEval+ anchor with this 35B model: first-sample 138/164, oracle any@5 144/164, recoverable only 6/164, 5/164, 4/164 across seeds (~3.7pp) -- the paper explicitly declines to use HumanEval+ as its code selector benchmark for that reason.
small_k_evidence: Yes -- the entire paper is run at k=5, the only rigorous small-k selection audit I found. Qwen3.5-9B pool on GPQA shrinks recoverable mass to 0.67% with 94.44% identical pools.
small_model_evidence: Partially: Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma-3-4B-it are listed as supplementary models, but Gemma-3-4B-it appears only in robustness/routing analyses with NO dedicated metrics. Sub-8B per-model selector gains are NOT REPORTED.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the paper that most threatens our novelty framing and most validates our audit discipline. Its ordering is ours: visible/public tests do the heavy lifting (69% of recoverable mass, zero harm), generated-test verification is coverage- and fidelity-limited (23%), and LLM/learned selectors buy little and actively HARM 4.7-5.7% of already-correct answers. Two concrete actions. First, we must report HARM (already-correct answers broken by selection) as a first-class metric alongside the paired difference; our current audit does not. Second, its HumanEval+ finding -- oracle gap ~3.7pp at k=5 on a strong model, too small to study -- is why our informative 230-task band and our weak 3B receiver (gap 7.37pp) are actually a methodological asset, not a limitation: we have recoverable mass where frontier setups do not. Cite it for that inversion. Its coverage bottleneck for generated tests (35.77% of rows activate) is the number to beat with input synthesis.

title: Dynamic Scaling of Unit Tests for Code Reward Modeling (CodeRM)
what_it_does: Trains CodeRM-8B to generate unit tests, then selects among N=100 candidates by majority voting over generated-test execution results. Crucially its Table 1 is a clean head-to-head of a LEARNED SCALAR reward model against execution-based selection on HumanEval+ and MBPP+.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED. N=100 throughout; the paper has no low-N scaling curve (its Figure 5 varies the number of unit tests, not the number of candidates).
small_model_evidence: Policy model Llama3-8B-Instruct is the smallest; nothing under 8B, nothing quantized.
bearing_on_our_decision: The single most useful row in this literature for us: on MBPP+ with an 8B policy, a trained scalar reward model LOSES to doing nothing (-0.80), and again loses with GPT-4o-mini (-2.59), while CodeT (generated tests + agreement) gains +10.00. That is published evidence that a learned selector fails on MBPP -- our benchmark. But the same table is a warning about our specific plan: PURE cross-candidate execution agreement, MBR-Exec, gains only +0.80 on MBPP+ at N=100, versus +6.72 on HumanEval+. MBPP tasks are short and their outputs are low-entropy, so output clusters are less discriminative; the +10.00 on MBPP+ comes from GENERATED TESTS, not from candidate-vs-candidate agreement. Decision consequence: our execution-agreement arm must include synthesised INPUT diversity (the CodeT/CodeRM ingredient), not just clustering on the one visible MBPP input, or we should expect roughly +0.008 on the MBPP half of our pool.

title: Scaling Agentic Verifier for Competitive Coding
venue_date: arXiv:2602.04254, 4 Feb 2026 (preprint)
what_it_does: Trains an execution-based agent to search for discriminative test INPUTS, then reranks by behavioural discrepancy. Reports Best@8 and Best@64 against vanilla, a grading reward model, CodeT, CodeRM, and a 'Random Generator' baseline (random input sampling + cross-candidate output agreement).
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, Best@8, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507. USACO: Vanilla 62.8, CodeT 68.5, CodeRM 68.7, Random Generator 69.7, Agentic Verifier 73.1. LiveCodeBench: 66.2 / 72.7 / 71.2 / 70.7 / 73.6. OJBench: 28.9 / 31.6 / 32.0 / 33.4 / 33.5. ICPC-Eval: 16.6 / 21.6 / 21.3 / 22.4 / 23.1. CodeForces: 33.2 / 38.6 / 38.9 / 39.5 / 43.0. Overall gains over vanilla +4.6 to +13.2. The grading reward model is inconsistent and sometimes below vanilla (e.g. 61.9, -0.9, on USACO Best@64). INFERRED: the naive 'Random Generator' (random inputs + execution agreement, no training) beats the trained CodeRM on 4 of 5 benchmarks at Best@8 and beats CodeT on 4 of 5, at zero training cost.
small_k_evidence: Yes -- Best@8 is reported as a primary setting on five benchmarks, which is exactly our planned k=8. This is the only paper I found that reports a full selector comparison AT k=8.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED. Policy models are Qwen3-30B-A3B (30B MoE, 3B active) and Qwen3-235B-A22B. Nothing under 8B dense.
bearing_on_our_decision: The strongest k=8 evidence that our untested candidate is the right one to test: at Best@8, random input generation plus cross-candidate output agreement -- which needs no training and no hidden tests -- gains +4.5 to +6.9 points and beats a trained reward model on 4 of 5 benchmarks, while the grading reward model can go NEGATIVE. This also tells us where the remaining headroom is (adversarial/discriminative input search, +3.4 more on USACO than random inputs), which is a cheap follow-on arm for us: generate inputs that SPLIT the candidate set rather than random inputs. Caveat for our regime: competitive-programming tasks have rich structured outputs where agreement discriminates well; MBPP does not (see CodeRM).

title: Improving Code Generation via Small Language Model-as-a-judge
venue_date: arXiv:2602.11911, 13 Feb 2026; ICSE 2026 (48th ICSE)
what_it_does: Fine-tunes sub-4B models as code-correctness judges and uses them to rerank 10 candidates from small generators. The closest paper in the literature to our exact model scale and our exact k.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER. Judge agreement with functional correctness (Cohen's kappa, fine-tuned): Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B 0.45, Qwen2.5-Coder-3B 0.57, Llama-3.2-3B 0.46, Gemma-3-4B 0.49; GPT-4.1-mini zero-shot 0.54; RankEF 0.40. Reranking pass@1 with 10 candidates and 1 judge (SLM-judge / RankEF / log-likelihood / random): DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B 0.447 / 0.366 / 0.336 / 0.324; OpenCoder-1.5B 0.473 / 0.432 / 0.401 / 0.374; Qwen2.5-Coder-3B 0.521 / 0.452 / 0.397 / 0.377; Phi-4-mini-4B 0.406 / 0.331 / 0.221 / 0.189; Gemma-3-4B 0.472 / 0.430 / 0.433 / 0.424. INFERRED: the fine-tuned judge beats random by +12.3 to +21.7 points (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B: +14.4), and beats log-likelihood by +3.9 to +18.5.
small_k_evidence: Yes -- k=10 candidates, the closest published k to our 8.
small_model_evidence: Yes -- generators 1.3B to 4B, judges 0.5B to 4B. This is the only paper I found operating entirely under 8B. Benchmarks: HumanEval, MBPP (Java), CoderEval. No oracle/pass@10 ceiling is reported, so the fraction of the oracle gap recovered is NOT FOUND.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the paper that most endangers our null. It shows that at k=10, with 1.3B-4B generators, a CHEAP LEARNED SELECTOR recovers a large absolute gain (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B: 0.377 random -> 0.521). Our claim therefore cannot be 'no learned selector recovers the gap'; it must be the narrower, defensible claim we actually measured: 'a learned selector over CHEAP STATIC FEATURES, cross-fitted, recovers none of it' -- static AST/length/token features are not what this paper uses; it fine-tunes a code LM on correctness labels. Two things blunt it as a threat. First, the judge REQUIRES supervised fine-tuning on the same task distribution (correctness labels from executed tests), which is exactly the label access our design forbids and our compute budget cannot afford. Second, it reports NO execution-agreement baseline and no visible-test filtering baseline -- its 'random' baseline is 0.377, far below our own filtering baseline of 0.7455, so the comparison that matters to us (learned judge vs execution agreement) is absent. We should say so explicitly; it is a gap in the evidence, and it is the head-to-head our experiment would supply.

title: Coder Reviewer Reranking for Code Generation
what_it_does: Reranks by the product p(code|instruction) x p(instruction|code) -- an execution-free, training-free likelihood reranker -- against MBR-Exec (execution agreement) across 6 datasets and 8 models from 3 families, with executability filtering.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, k=25 samples, with executability filtering. HumanEval (Codex002 / InCoder-6B / CodeGen-16B): Random 49.2 / 16.0 / 32.2; Coder 45.1 / 20.1 / 33.5; MBR-Exec 50.5 / 20.7 / 35.8; Coder-Reviewer 56.7 / 23.5 / 40.0; Normalised Coder-Reviewer 62.5 / 22.0 / 39.6. MBPP: Random 58.1 / 19.6 / 39.3; Coder 60.2 / 23.4 / 41.5; MBR-Exec 63.0 / 26.7 / 47.3; Coder-Reviewer 66.4 / 26.1 / 46.2; N.Coder-Reviewer 66.2 / 24.1 / 45.4. Headline claim up to 17% absolute over Coder-only reranking.
small_k_evidence: k=25 (50 bootstrap runs). No k<=10 setting. NOT REPORTED at small k.
small_model_evidence: Yes: InCoder-1B and 6B, CodeGen-2B/6B/16B, Codex-Cushman 12B. On MBPP, MBR-Exec BEATS Coder-Reviewer for both smaller models -- InCoder-6B 26.7 vs 26.1 and CodeGen-16B 47.3 vs 46.2 -- while Coder-Reviewer wins on the 175B Codex002 (66.4 vs 63.0).
bearing_on_our_decision: Published evidence that an execution-free reranker FAILS to beat execution agreement specifically as model size falls, on MBPP: MBR-Exec wins on InCoder-6B and CodeGen-16B and loses only on Codex-175B. The likelihood signal Coder-Reviewer exploits is a property of strong models; our 3B/7B q4_k_m receivers sit below every model where it works. This is the size-scaling argument for preferring execution agreement in our regime, and it pairs with DOCE (where Filter+CR added only +0.9/+0.2 on a 6.7B model). Note also that DOCE re-measured CR on DeepSeek-6.7B and found it BELOW greedy (70.3 vs 76.8 on HumanEval+), i.e. the method does not replicate downward in scale.

title: LEVER: Learning to Verify Language-to-Code Generation with Execution
what_it_does: Trains a per-dataset verifier on (NL input, program, execution result) to score candidates, and reranks by verifier probability x generation probability. The canonical learned-verifier-for-code paper, and the main existence proof that a learned verifier can beat execution agreement.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, k=100 samples at both training and inference. MBPP with Codex code-davinci-002: Greedy 62.0 test / 61.1 dev; Error-Pruning+MaxLikelihood 60.2 / 62.2; MBR-Exec 63.0 test; Reviewer 66.9 test; LEVER 68.9 +/-0.4 test, 75.4 +/-0.7 dev; ORACLE 79.0 dev. Overall gains 4.6% to 10.9% over base LLMs. Ablation: removing execution results from the verifier input costs 5.6 points -- i.e. the learned part is carried by EXECUTION features, not by static code features. Smaller models (Spider / GSM8k only, MBPP NOT REPORTED for them): InCoder-6B Spider 24.1 greedy -> 54.1 LEVER; CodeGen-16B Spider 24.6 -> 51.0; InCoder-6B GSM8k 3.1 -> 11.9; CodeGen-16B GSM8k 7.1 -> 22.1. Cross-LLM transfer of the verifier (Table 8): Codex->InCoder +4.7, Codex->CodeGen +4.4, InCoder<->CodeGen +12.9 to +13.3 on Spider. INFERRED: on MBPP dev, LEVER closes (75.4-62.2)/(79.0-62.2) = 78.6% of the post-error-pruning oracle gap, and beats MBR-Exec by +5.9 points on test.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED. k=100 everywhere; no low-k ablation.
small_model_evidence: InCoder-6B and CodeGen-16B are evaluated, but ONLY on Spider and GSM8k -- the paper gives no MBPP or HumanEval numbers for any sub-8B model.
bearing_on_our_decision: LEVER is the headline counterexample to our null and must be addressed head-on, but three of its properties put it out of our reach and out of our claim's scope. (1) It needs k=100 draws per task for verifier TRAINING as well as inference; at 909 receiver calls/hour, 100 draws x 561 tasks x 2 models is ~123,000 calls, roughly 135 contended hours -- flatly outside our budget. (2) The verifier is trained PER DATASET on programs sampled from the same task distribution with execution labels; transfer is only shown across LLMs, never across datasets, and the paper notes transfer degrades when positive-label rates differ -- which is exactly the 3B-vs-7B mismatch we would face. (3) Its own ablation says the signal is execution-derived (-5.6 without execution results), which is why our static-feature model recovered nothing and is entirely consistent with our null rather than contradicting it. The correct write-up is: LEVER shows the gap is recoverable WITH k=100 and in-distribution supervised labels; we show it is not recoverable at k<=8 from static features without labels; execution agreement is the untested middle.

title: CodeT: Code Generation with Generated Tests
