what_it_does: Generates test cases with the same LLM, executes all candidates on them, and selects by DUAL execution agreement -- consensus on generated-test outcomes plus agreement with other candidates of the same functional behaviour. The direct ancestor of our proposed agreement-clustering arm.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, n=100 code samples for HumanEval/MBPP (50 for APPS, 1000 for CodeContests). HumanEval pass@1 baseline -> CodeT: code-cushman-001 33.5 -> 44.5; code-davinci-002 47.0 -> 65.8; InCoder-6B 16.4 -> 20.6; CodeGen-Mono-16B 29.7 -> 36.7. MBPP pass@1 baseline -> CodeT: code-cushman-001 45.9 -> 55.4; code-davinci-002 58.1 -> 67.7; InCoder-6B 21.3 -> 34.4; CodeGen-16B 42.4 -> 49.5. AlphaCode-C clustering (agreement only, no generated tests): HumanEval 39.6 / 55.1 / 17.7; MBPP 51.5 / 62.0 / 26.7 -- consistently BELOW CodeT. Oracle pass@100 code-davinci-002: HumanEval 92.1, MBPP 84.5; InCoder-6B HumanEval 47.5, MBPP 66.2; CodeGen-16B HumanEval 73.7, MBPP 79.1. Test-count ablation: 10 generated tests still give +4.3 (cushman) and +9.5 (davinci-002) on HumanEval. INFERRED gap closure vs pass@100 oracle: InCoder-6B MBPP (34.4-21.3)/(66.2-21.3) = 29.2%; InCoder-6B HumanEval 4.2/31.1 = 13.5%; CodeGen-16B MBPP 7.1/36.7 = 19.3%; code-davinci-002 MBPP 9.6/26.4 = 36.4%.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED for the number of CODE samples -- the paper has no ablation below n=100 on candidate count (its low-count ablation is over TEST cases, where 10 tests suffice). This is a real gap: the most-cited execution-agreement result for code has never been measured at k<=10.
small_model_evidence: Yes -- InCoder-6B is the best sub-8B data point in this literature: MBPP 21.3 -> 34.4 (+13.1), the LARGEST absolute gain of any model in the paper, consistent with weak models having more recoverable mass.
bearing_on_our_decision: Two decisive facts. First, dual agreement beats pure clustering everywhere: AlphaCode-C (candidate-vs-candidate agreement alone) is 3.5 to 10.7 points below CodeT on the same pools -- so our planned design (cluster on common inputs) should NOT be run in its pure form; it should include LLM-generated test cases, since 10 tests already buy most of the effect and 10 tests x 561 tasks is ~5,600 calls, about 6 hours, affordable. Second, the sub-8B signal is encouraging: InCoder-6B gains +13.1 on MBPP, 29.2% of its oracle gap. But everything is at n=100 candidates; the candidate-count dependence that decides our k=8 case is simply NOT MEASURED in the field's most-cited agreement paper. That absence is itself a contribution we can make.

title: Universal Self-Consistency for Large Language Model Generation
venue_date: arXiv:2311.17311, 29 Nov 2023 (preprint; OpenReview LjsjHF7nAN)
what_it_does: Concatenates all sampled responses and asks the LLM itself to pick the most consistent one -- an execution-free LLM selector -- evaluated against execution-based voting on code/SQL generation.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, BIRD-SQL execution accuracy: greedy 42.4, random selection 41.9, execution-based self-consistency (SC-Exec) 45.6, USC 45.5. Valid-efficiency score: greedy 44.4, random 44.0, SC-Exec 48.1, USC 48.8. The paper's own framing is that USC 'matches the execution-based voting performance' -- it does not exceed it on accuracy (45.5 vs 45.6). ARCADE results are reported in the same Table 2 but the exact values are NOT FOUND in the sources I could read.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- the number of sampled responses for the code/SQL tables is NOT FOUND in the accessible text.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED; models are PaLM-2 / GPT-3.5-class. Nothing under 8B.
bearing_on_our_decision: A clean, citable statement that the best an LLM-as-selector achieves is PARITY with execution agreement (45.5 vs 45.6), never superiority, on a code-adjacent task. For us this closes off the 'just ask the 7B model to pick' arm: parity with execution agreement is the ceiling even for a frontier-class selector, and our receivers are far weaker judges than PaLM-2. Combined with the Oracle-Gap paper's 4.69% harm rate for LLM selectors, an LLM-judge arm is dominated -- spend the compute on execution agreement instead.

title: ACECODER: Acing Coder RL via Automated Test-Case Synthesis
what_it_does: Synthesises 1.38M test cases over 87.1K questions (AceCode-87K), builds preference pairs from pass rates, and trains AceCode-RM (7B and 32B) with Bradley-Terry loss for best-of-N reranking.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, best-of-32. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: greedy HumanEval 68.9, MBPP 67.2; AceCode-RM-7B 79.9 / 76.2; AceCode-RM-32B 81.7 / 72.8. Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct: greedy HumanEval 91.5, MBPP 82.8; AceCode-RM-7B 90.9 / 87.8; AceCode-RM-32B 90.2 / 87.8. Headline: average ~10 points for Llama-3.1-8B-Ins and ~5 points for Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Ins via best-of-32. INFERRED: on HumanEval with the 7B Qwen policy, best-of-32 with the trained RM is -0.6 BELOW greedy (90.9 vs 91.5) and the 32B RM is -1.3 below (90.2), i.e. the trained reward model is net harmful on the benchmark half where the model is already strong; the entire average gain comes from MBPP (+5.0).
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED below N=16; best-of-16 and best-of-32 only.
small_model_evidence: Policy models are 7B and 8B (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct is one of our own receiver families, unquantized). Reward models are 7B and 32B. Nothing at 3B.
bearing_on_our_decision: The most directly comparable receiver in the literature -- Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct -- and it shows the pattern our audit found: a trained outcome reward model, trained on 87K in-distribution questions with 1.38M synthesised tests, still goes NEGATIVE on HumanEval (90.9 vs 91.5 greedy) at best-of-32. It only helps on MBPP (+5.0). Two consequences. (1) Our 7B receiver's small selection gap (0.0351) is consistent with the field: there is little recoverable mass on HumanEval for a competent 7B coder, so we should PRE-REGISTER the expectation that the 7B arm is underpowered and put our statistical weight on the 3B (gap 0.0737) and on the MBPP half. (2) The training cost -- 87K questions, 1.38M tests -- is the price of a learned selector that still cannot beat greedy on half our pool. That is the decisive cost-benefit argument for the execution-agreement arm.

title: Enhancing Large Language Models in Coding Through Multi-Perspective Self-Consistency (MPSC)
venue_date: arXiv:2309.17272, 29 Sep 2023 (preprint)
what_it_does: Builds a tripartite graph over generated solutions, specifications and test cases, and scores candidates by inter-perspective and intra-perspective consistency -- an unsupervised but structured selector -- compared directly against CodeT and self-consistency.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, 200 solutions + 100 specifications + 500 test cases per problem, GPT-3.5-Turbo. HumanEval pass@1: baseline 68.38, self-consistency 73.86, CodeT 78.05, MPSC-weighted-cardinality 85.98. MBPP pass@1: baseline 66.80, self-consistency 71.70, CodeT 71.90, MPSC 73.17. Note the independent re-measurement in CodeRM's Table 1 at N=100 is much less favourable to MPSC: HumanEval+ Llama3-8B MPSC 59.72 (+6.14) vs CodeT 65.30 (+11.72); MBPP+ MPSC 53.32 (+4.12) vs CodeT 59.20 (+10.00).
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- 200 solutions per problem, the largest budget of any paper here.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED at small scale in the original (GPT-3.5/GPT-4/CodeLlama/WizardCoder), but CodeRM re-ran it on Llama3-8B, where it underperforms CodeT by 5.6 to 5.9 points.
bearing_on_our_decision: Counter-evidence worth reporting honestly: a structured consistency selector CAN beat execution agreement (85.98 vs 78.05 on HumanEval) -- but only at 200 solutions, 100 specifications and 500 tests per problem, i.e. ~800 generations per task versus our 8, and when re-measured by an independent group at N=100 on an 8B policy it LOSES to CodeT on both benchmarks. Treat as a ceiling result that does not transfer to k<=8, and cite the CodeRM re-measurement as the reason.

title: ACES: Who Tests the Tests? Leave-One-Out AUC Consistency for Code Generation
venue_date: arXiv:2604.03922 (v2 dated 12 Jul 2026), preprint
what_it_does: Fixes the circularity in generated-test selection by weighting each test by its leave-one-out AUC -- whether the test's pass/fail pattern agrees with the ranking induced by the other tests -- rather than counting votes. Proves the expected LOO-AUC is proportional to a test's ability to separate correct from incorrect code. Two variants: closed-form ACES-C and iterative ACES-O.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, HumanEval with GPT-3.5-Turbo, ~200 candidates and ~500 tests per problem. Pass@1 / Pass@2 / Pass@5: baseline 68.38 / 76.24 / 83.15; CodeT 78.05 / 78.05 / 78.30; majority voting 80.49 / 82.93 / 83.54; ACES-C 82.93 / 82.93 / 82.93; ACES-O 84.15 / 85.98 / 86.59. Also evaluated on HumanEval+ and MBPP (427 problems). The paper does not quantify remaining oracle-gap closure.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- ~200 candidates, ~500 tests.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- GPT-3.5-Turbo generation; no sub-8B generator.
bearing_on_our_decision: The current state of the art in the exact sub-problem we would hit if we go the generated-test route: our 3B receiver's generated assertions will be mostly wrong, and ACES is the principled way to down-weight bad tests without knowing which code is correct. Two uses for us. (1) If the execution-agreement arm underperforms, ACES-style LOO-AUC test weighting is the cheapest documented next step -- it is pure post-processing on an execution matrix we will already have computed, costing zero extra receiver calls. (2) Note that CodeT's pass@1 is FLAT across pass@1/2/5 (78.05/78.05/78.30) while ACES-O rises -- evidence that hard-consensus selectors collapse the candidate set and lose the ability to exploit additional budget, which is directly relevant to our STOPPING question.

title: Semantic Voting: Execution-Grounded Consensus for LLM Code Generation
venue_date: arXiv:2605.08680v1, 12 May 2026 (preprint)
what_it_does: Votes over execution BEHAVIOUR (outputs on synthesised inputs) rather than over output text or normalised ASTs, on HumanEval+ (164) and MBPP+ (375-378), with 50 candidates and 50 synthesised test inputs (10 input sketches x 5 instantiations).
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, HumanEval+, N=50 candidates, D=50 inputs, low thinking level. Gemini-3.1-Pro: output-pattern majority vote 75.0, weighted vote 98.8, MBR-Exec 97.6, SemanticVote 98.8. Gemini-3-Flash: 64.6 / 96.3 / 95.1 / 95.7. Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite: 51.8 / 92.7 / 92.7 / 92.1. Headline: 'the best execution-based selector exceeds output-pattern majority voting by 19-52 percentage points on every configuration' across all 18 tested combinations. Does NOT evaluate random selection, LLM judges, reward models, CodeT or plain self-consistency as baselines.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- N=50 primary, N=100 ablation.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- three Gemini preview endpoints, parameter counts undisclosed; nothing identifiable as under 8B.
bearing_on_our_decision: Useful for two design details and one caution. Design: (a) it confirms that semantic/execution voting needs SYNTHESISED INPUTS, and that 50 inputs from 10 sketches x 5 instantiations suffices -- a concrete, cheap recipe for the inputs our MBPP tasks do not give us; (b) it shows the naive form of our idea (voting on output PATTERNS/text) is 19-52 points worse than executing, so we must cluster on executed behaviour, not on output strings. Caution: on HumanEval+/MBPP+ with these models MBR-Exec, weighted voting and SemanticVote are all within ~1 point of each other at 92-99% -- the benchmarks are saturated, so the paper cannot distinguish methods and its numbers say nothing about a 3B receiver at 72%.

title: CodeScore: Evaluating Code Generation by Learning Code Execution
what_it_does: Trains an LLM-based metric (UniCE framework) to predict PassRatio and Executability from the NL and/or reference plus the candidate, WITHOUT executing anything at inference. Reports up to 58.87% improvement in correlation with functional correctness over other code-evaluation metrics, and a ~1000x execution-time saving.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: up to 58.87% relative improvement in correlation with functional correctness versus other code evaluation metrics; three input formats (Ref-only, NL-only, Ref&NL); no test cases or execution needed at inference. The decisive number for us is the INDEPENDENT re-measurement in DOCE (Table 4, DeepSeekCoder-6.7B, n=50, HumanEval+): CodeScore as a reranker scores 63.6 versus Random 65.1 and Greedy 76.8, and Filter+CodeScore 78.4 versus Filter alone 78.7 -- i.e. it is BELOW random and it DEGRADES visible-test filtering.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED in the original; the DOCE re-measurement is at n=50 with an n in {1,5,10,20,25,50} sweep for MBR-Exec only.
small_model_evidence: The DOCE re-measurement is on DeepSeekCoder-6.7B-Instruct and CodeLlama-7B-Instruct -- sub-8B, and the result is negative.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the cleanest published instance of exactly our finding: a TRAINED, execution-free scorer that correlates well with correctness in isolation (up to +58.87% correlation, TOSEM-published) nevertheless fails as a SELECTOR on a real candidate pool from a sub-8B model -- below random, and negative on top of visible-test filtering. It is the citation that makes our four null fractions (-0.18, -0.06, 0.00, 0.00, all intervals covering zero) an expected replication rather than a suspected bug in our pipeline. It also states the general lesson we should lead with: high average correlation with correctness does not imply discriminative power WITHIN a pool of candidates for the same task, because within-task variance is what selection consumes.

title: On the Robustness of LLMs' Internal Representation of Code Correctness
venue_date: arXiv:2608.08266v1, 8 Aug 2026 (preprint)
what_it_does: Audits linear probing of hidden states as a cheap, execution-free correctness signal for code, systematically varying direction-construction method, prompt framing and read-out location, on four 7-8B instruction-tuned code LLMs.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER. Models: Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, OpenCoder-8B-Instruct, CodeLlama-7B-Instruct. Benchmarks: HumanEval (164), BigCodeBench (1,140), MBPP+ as out-of-distribution. In-distribution selection accuracy spans 19.0-77.4% on BigCodeBench and 29.7-79.4% on HumanEval ACROSS CONFIGURATIONS -- i.e. the configuration choice, not the method, dominates. Controlled-pair (mutation-only) fitting transfers badly: BigCodeBench 19.6% vs a 56.7% in-distribution baseline; HumanEval 47.6% vs 52.8%. Paper's conclusions: 'no single configuration is best'; only mean-diff construction generalises consistently; isolating the bug-causing mutation does NOT help, because a direction that separates a program from a perturbed copy is not suited to judging an independent candidate.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- it measures pairwise/selection accuracy, not best-of-N gains at a given k. Best-of-N pass@1 gains are NOT MEASURED.
small_model_evidence: Yes -- all four models are 7-8B, the closest match to our 7B receiver of any probing paper.
bearing_on_our_decision: Directly generalises our null one level deeper: not only do cheap STATIC features fail, so do cheap probes of the model's own INTERNAL states, on 7-8B code models, with the added finding that the apparent signal is an artefact of how the probe was constructed and does not survive the switch from perturbed-copy pairs to independent candidates -- which is precisely the switch our selection task requires. Two uses: (1) it forecloses the 'read the hidden state / use the logits' arm before we spend an hour on it, which matters at 909 calls/hour; (2) it tells us to distrust any positive result we obtain from a single feature/hyperparameter configuration, and to keep the cross-fitting and interval reporting we already do.

title: Shrinking the Generation-Verification Gap with Weak Verifiers (Weaver)
venue_date: arXiv:2506.18203, 22 Jun 2025 (preprint)
what_it_does: Ensembles 33 off-the-shelf reward models and LM judges (7B-72B) with weak-supervision statistics to estimate per-verifier accuracy without full labels, then reranks; also distils the ensemble into a 400M ModernBERT-Large cross-encoder.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, K=100 generations, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct generator (also Llama-3.1-8B), on MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-College, MMLU-Pro (code generation is NOT a main benchmark). Average accuracy: majority voting 72.2, best single weak verifier 72.7, Weaver 87.7, oracle pass@100 91.9, o3-mini frontier baseline 86.7. Closes the generation-verification gap by 12.8% for 8B models and 16.0% for 70B relative to majority voting; 14.5-17.9% over first-sample. Requires a small labelled dev set of ~1% of the test set (5-10 query-answer pairs) to calibrate, and no gradient finetuning on full labels.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- K=100 primary, scaling up to 2^10.
small_model_evidence: An 8B generator is included, but verifiers are 7B-72B and the reported ensemble needs 33 of them; the distilled 400M verifier is the only cheap artefact.
bearing_on_our_decision: The most important negative number here is the BASELINE, not the method: the BEST SINGLE weak verifier out of 33 reward models and LM judges beats majority voting by 0.5 points (72.7 vs 72.2). Any single off-the-shelf reward model we could download is, on average, worth half a point over voting -- that is the realistic value of the 'just add a reward model' arm for us, and it is far below our 0.0737 target. Weaver only works by ensembling 33 verifiers at K=100, which is ~33x our entire compute budget. Code is not a main benchmark, so even its positive result does not transfer. Use it to justify not running a reward-model arm at all.

title: Lightweight Reranking for Language Model Generations (UCS / Consensus-WUCS)
venue_date: arXiv:2307.06857, Jul 2023 (preprint; later ACL-track)
what_it_does: The cheapest possible agreement selector: no execution, no training, no extra model calls -- represent each generation as a binary token-presence vector and pick the generation with the highest average pairwise inner product with the others. Weighted and consensus variants add token probabilities.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, 125 generations for code tasks (50 for others). HumanEval with Codex-davinci-002: Random 43.5 -> UCS 53.9 -> Consensus-WUCS 56.8 (+13.3 over random). MBPP with Codex-davinci-002: Random 53.6 -> UCS 58.0 -> Consensus-WUCS 59.4 (+5.8 over random). Consensus-WUCS matched or exceeded Normalised Coder-Reviewer in 6 of 15 experiments (40%). Ablations cover sample counts from 5 to 100. Models: Codex-davinci-001/002, Codex-Cushman (12B), Llama-13B, Llama-30B, GPT-J.
small_k_evidence: Partially -- ablations 'ranging from 5 to 100' samples are described, but the exact per-k values for code are NOT FOUND in the sources I could read. This is the only agreement-style paper that claims to ablate down to 5.
small_model_evidence: Llama-13B and Codex-Cushman-12B are the smallest; nothing under 8B. NOT REPORTED for sub-8B.
bearing_on_our_decision: Establishes the free floor our execution-agreement arm must clear: lexical agreement among candidates, at literally zero marginal cost (no execution, no inputs to synthesise, no training), already buys +5.8 on MBPP and +13.3 on HumanEval over random and matches a likelihood reranker 40% of the time. Two consequences for the design: (1) add lexical-agreement (UCS) as a CONTROL arm -- if execution agreement does not beat UCS, the execution machinery is not earning its compute; (2) note that a large part of what 'agreement clustering' buys may be pure redundancy-counting rather than semantic equivalence, so the pre-registered comparison must be execution-agreement vs UCS vs visible-filter, not merely execution-agreement vs random.

title: Don't Overthink It: Inter-Rollout Action Agreement as a Free Adaptive-Compute Signal for LLM Agents (TrACE)
venue_date: arXiv:2604.08369v1, 9 Apr 2026, preprint (Stanford, single author)
what_it_does: Uses inter-rollout agreement on the next action as a training-free difficulty proxy: sample k_init=2, stop when agreement alpha >= tau_high=0.75, else keep sampling to k_max. Exactly the 'agreement as a stopping signal' idea, on exactly our hardware and model.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: receiver is Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Q4_K_M, CPU inference -- the same model, same quantization, same runtime class as ours. k_init=2, k_max in {4,8}. GSM8K (n=50, 1 seed): greedy 0.780 [0.660,0.880] at 1.00 call; SC-4 0.820 [0.720,0.920] at 4.00; SC-8 0.840 [0.740,0.940] at 8.00; TrACE-4 0.820 at 2.68 calls; TrACE-8 0.840 at 3.56 calls. MiniHouse (n=30 x 3 seeds): greedy 0.367 at 5.96 calls; SC-4 and SC-8 both 0.378 at 24.93 / 48.62 calls; TrACE-4 0.378 at 14.49; TrACE-8 0.378 at 16.09. INFERRED savings at matched accuracy: 33.0% (4), 55.5% (8) on GSM8K; 41.9% (4), 66.9% (8) on MiniHouse. INFERRED: accuracy delta is exactly 0.000 in all four matched comparisons -- this is a pure cost result, not an accuracy result.
small_k_evidence: YES -- the only paper found that runs an agreement-based stopping rule entirely inside k<=8. k_init=2, k_max=4 and 8. MEASURED-IN-PAPER.
small_model_evidence: YES -- Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct Q4_K_M on CPU. MEASURED-IN-PAPER. This is the only sub-8B quantized receiver found anywhere in the stopping literature.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the closest thing to prior art on our stopping half, and it is weak enough to beat: n=50 GSM8K on a single seed, 95% CIs of width ~0.21, no code benchmark, no oracle/pass@k accounting, no formal guarantee, agreement measured on actions not on execution outputs. Our 561-task audited pool with a 230-task informative band and paired CIs is an order of magnitude better powered. Take away: (a) an agreement-triggered stop at k<=8 on a quantized 3B does save 33-56% of calls at zero accuracy loss, so the stopping half of our question has a real positive answer; (b) it saves compute, it does not recover accuracy -- consistent with our own adaptive-BoN result beating the feedback loop on cost, not on correctness. Cite it as the baseline and differentiate on code, execution-output agreement, oracle accounting, and power.

title: Majority Voting for Code Generation (Functional Majority Vote, FMV)
venue_date: arXiv:2604.15618v1, 17 Apr 2026, preprint (ETH Zurich; Hubotter, Bagatella, Krause et al.)
what_it_does: Execution-agreement selection for code done properly: execute every candidate on every generated input, build an execution vector per candidate, pick the candidate maximizing pairwise functional agreement with the ensemble. This is precisely the 'largest output-agreement cluster' method we have not yet tested.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER (Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, LiveCodeBench-v6, N=64): mean@64 (average single-sample accuracy) 30.8 +/- 3.2; FMV 41.2 +/- 4.3; best@64 (oracle) 48.9 +/- 1.0. Figure 2 comparison at N=64: base mean@64 37.7; Semantic Voting 48.1; GenCluster 52.7; FMV on par or better than GenCluster. At N=32 FMV is above 40%. Scaling analysis at N in {32,64,128}. INFERRED, and this is the single most decision-relevant number in this whole search: execution agreement recovers (41.2-30.8)/(48.9-30.8) = 10.4/18.1 = 57.5% of the oracle selection gap for a 4B model at N=64 on LiveCodeBench-v6.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED. Primary N=64; scaling only down to N=32. No k<=8 experiment anywhere in the paper.
small_model_evidence: PARTIAL -- Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. The 4B is under 8B, but unquantized and a 2507-generation model, i.e. considerably stronger than Qwen2.5-3B q4_k_m.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the number to reconcile against. If execution agreement transferred at its published efficiency, it would recover 0.575 x 0.0737 = 0.0424 absolute on our 3B (INFERRED) -- but note that our visible-assertion adaptive rule ALREADY recovers (0.7455-0.7169)/0.0737 = 38.8% of the gap (INFERRED), so agreement must clear 38.8% just to tie what we have for free. The head-room above our current rule is only 0.8192-0.7455 = 0.0451 absolute (INFERRED). Two further cautions: their gap is 18.1 points and ours is 7.37, so there is 2.5x less signal to harvest; and their k is 64 while ours is 8. Also note they do not use HumanEval or MBPP at all, and do not report oracle-gap fractions themselves -- the 57.5% is ours to compute, which means the k<=8 / MBPP / quantized-3B cell is genuinely empty and is ours to fill.

title: Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-stopping Self-Consistency (ESC)
venue_date: arXiv:2401.10480, ICLR 2024 (published conference paper), 19 Jan 2024
what_it_does: Window-based agreement stopping: sample in sequential windows of size w; stop as soon as one window is unanimous (zero entropy). The canonical cheap stopping rule, and the only one with real MBPP numbers at small total budget.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER. MBPP, GPT-3.5-Turbo, w=5, Table 4: at L=10 SC 61.96 / ESC 61.96 (delta 0.00) with L-hat 5.62; L=15 61.96/61.96 with 6.02; L=20 62.04/62.02 (-0.02) with 6.32; L=25 62.15/62.11 (-0.04) with 6.57; L=30 62.18/62.15 (-0.03) with 6.79. Main table savings: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CSQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%. Theory: one-proportion z-test; for w=8 the probability that early stopping changes the vote is <= 2e-3 (a bound, not a proof of unbiasedness). INFERRED: on MBPP the stopping rule saves 43.8% of calls at L=10 and its absorbed cost is nearly flat in L (5.62 -> 6.79 as L goes 10 -> 30), so at our k=8 cap an ESC-style rule would spend roughly 5.4 draws, about 33% savings.
small_k_evidence: YES -- Table 4 runs MBPP at L=10 and L=15, and Appendix A.3 runs L=10 on GSM8K/CSQA/Letters. w=5 means the rule can first fire at draw 5, so it is operative inside k=8. MEASURED-IN-PAPER.
small_model_evidence: YES, and it is the warning shot. LLaMA-2-7B, L=10, MEASURED-IN-PAPER: GSM8K SC 20.74 / ESC 20.74, L-hat 8.99 (saves only 1.01 of 10 draws); Last Letters 21.21/21.21, L-hat 9.67 (saves 0.33); CSQA 66.89/66.89, L-hat 6.59. At L=20 on GSM8K the 7B spends 17.06 of 20. Compare GPT-4 at L=10: 5.79 on GSM8K.
bearing_on_our_decision: Two hard constraints for our design. (1) MBPP is in scope and the rule is accuracy-neutral there to within 0.04 points -- so we can safely bolt an agreement-stop onto our k=8 design without risking the 0.7455 we already have. (2) The LLaMA-2-7B rows show the failure mode that will bite us: a weak model's draws are rarely unanimous, so the agreement condition almost never fires and savings collapse from ~44% (GPT-3.5) to ~10% (7B) to ~3% (7B, high-diversity task). Our receivers are weaker than LLaMA-2-7B. Expect our agreement clusters to be fragmented, which cuts both ways: little stopping benefit, but possibly more discriminative signal for selection. Budget the experiment to measure cluster-size distribution first -- it is the cheap diagnostic that predicts whether either use of agreement can work.

title: Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning and Coding with LLMs
what_it_does: Lightweight posterior stopping criterion over the running answer counts, re-evaluated after every sample, non-uniformly spreading a fixed budget across questions. The original adaptive-consistency (ASC) baseline that everything since is measured against.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER (abstract-level): up to 7.9x reduction in sample budget with average accuracy drop < 0.1%, across 17 reasoning and code-generation benchmarks and 3 LLMs. NOT FOUND from the sources I could read: the per-benchmark code-generation table, the exact k_max, the average samples used, the stopping-rule family (Beta vs Dirichlet), and any behaviour at k<=10. The PDF would not render for extraction and the landing page carries only the abstract.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED in what I could read. The 7.9x figure implies a large k_max (a 7.9x cut from k<=8 is arithmetically impossible), so the headline result lives in the large-k regime.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- the three LLMs are not named on the abstract page.
bearing_on_our_decision: Cite as the required baseline and the origin of the ASC label that ESC/DSC/ReASC/Bayesian-stopping all benchmark against, but do not lean on its numbers: a 7.9x saving is only achievable when k_max is in the tens-to-hundreds, and our k=8 ceiling caps any stopping rule at 8x by construction and realistically at ~1.5x. The honest framing for our paper is that the entire adaptive-consistency line reports its wins at budgets 4-40x larger than ours, so the small-k cell is unclaimed.

title: When Does Learning to Stop Help? A Cost-Aware Study of Early Exits in Reasoning Models
venue_date: arXiv:2606.30852v1, announced 29 Jun 2026 (v1 dated 24 Aug 2026), preprint
what_it_does: Directly tests whether a LEARNED stopping rule beats simple scalar rules (confidence, entropy, stability) once the cost of the learned probe is charged, across five benchmarks and two model sizes. This is our exact methodological question asked of the stopping decision.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER. Where learning helps: GSM8K + Qwen3-32B peak gain +0.157 raw, but only +0.028 over the strongest scalar baseline, 95% CI [+0.002, +0.053]; MATH-500 + Qwen3-8B +0.023 over entropy exit, 95% CI [+0.005, +0.042]; MATH-500 + Qwen3-32B +0.005, not significant. Where it fails: AIME-90 -0.024 (8B) and -0.010 (32B); MMLU-Pro and GPQA -- learned stopper does not beat the strongest scalar baseline at either size. Cost accounting: GSM8K-32B with risk calibration shows 54.4% thinking-token savings collapsing to 32.5% total-token savings once probe overhead is charged; the authors call pure black-box API accounting 'uneconomical'. Quoted conclusion: on multiple-choice and very hard settings, scalar confidence, entropy or stability rules are competitive or stronger.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- this is about token-level early exit within a trace, not about k parallel draws.
small_model_evidence: PARTIAL -- smallest receivers are Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. Nothing under 7B.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is external corroboration of our own null result, from a different angle, with intervals. Our cross-fitted GBM and logistic model over cheap static features recovered fractions -0.18, -0.06, 0.00, 0.00 with all intervals covering zero; this paper finds that even a learned stopper with access to internal states beats the best one-line heuristic by at most +0.028 [+0.002,+0.053] in its best cell and loses in three of five. It also independently reproduces our adaptive-BoN-beats-feedback finding in spirit: the cheap rule is the strong baseline. Use it to justify not spending more compute on learned selectors over cheap features, and to justify spending it on the one execution-grounded signal instead. It also gives us the right honesty bar: report the learned rule's gain OVER the best simple rule, net of its own cost, with a CI -- not over the naive baseline.

title: Strategic Scaling of Test-Time Compute: A Bandit Learning Approach
venue_date: arXiv:2506.12721v2, v2 dated 24 Apr 2026, preprint (Zuo & Zhu)
what_it_does: Formulates per-query compute allocation as a multi-armed bandit where each arm is a compute budget, estimates query difficulty online, and allocates a total budget to maximize the fraction solved. The closest formal treatment of allocation at budgets in our range, with a proof.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER. Budgets tested: {4, 8, 16, 32} standard, and {1, 2, 3, 4} for Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite. Gains over uniform allocation: MATH-500 +11.10 points (15.04% relative) with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct AT BUDGET 8; AIME25 +10.82 (14.44% relative) with Qwen3-4B at budget 16; LiveCodeBench +11.23 (15.29% relative) with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B. Efficiency gains 1.82x to 4.00x versus uniform allocation. Theorem 1: their algorithm needs total budget Theta-tilde(sum_x 1/Delta_x) to answer all queries correctly w.p. >= 1-delta, versus Omega-tilde(max |S|/Delta_x) for uniform allocation.
small_k_evidence: YES, and it is the best small-budget evidence found. The headline MATH-500 gain is measured AT BUDGET 8, and the Gemini sweep goes down to budget 1. MEASURED-IN-PAPER.
small_model_evidence: YES -- Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and Qwen3-4B are both under 8B, alongside Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B and Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite. MEASURED-IN-PAPER.
bearing_on_our_decision: Most useful positive result in the search for the ALLOCATION half of our question. It establishes that at budget exactly 8, with sub-8B models, non-uniform difficulty-aware allocation buys +11 points over spreading the same budget uniformly -- which is a much larger effect than any selection rule recovers, and it is measured in our budget regime rather than extrapolated from k=64. It also supplies the formal object we need: a regret/budget bound in terms of per-query gaps Delta_x. Caveat before we lean on it: the gain is over UNIFORM allocation on a set of queries of mixed difficulty, i.e. it is largely the gain from not wasting draws on already-solved and hopeless tasks. Our audited pool already isolates a 230-task informative difficulty band, so we have partially banked this gain and must not double-count it -- the honest comparison is allocation within the informative band.

title: Optimal Stopping vs Best-of-N for Inference Time Optimization
venue_date: arXiv:2510.01394, 1 Oct 2025, preprint (Kalayci, Raman, Dughmi; cs.LG)
what_it_does: Casts best-of-N as Pandora's Box: each generation is a box opened at a cost with an uncertain reward, and the question is when to stop opening. Gives a UCB-style Pandora's Box algorithm for the unknown-distribution case.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: the adaptive rule matches non-adaptive best-of-N performance while using 15-35% fewer generations on average, on AlpacaFarm and HH-RLHF with multiple LLM/reward-model pairs. Guarantee: provably close to Weitzman's algorithm, which is optimal when the reward distribution is known. NOT FOUND: the exact N values, any N<=8 result, and the model sizes -- the landing page does not carry them.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the cleanest formal frame for our stopping question and it maps onto our setup almost exactly: each draw costs one receiver call (~4 seconds of our 909-calls-per-hour budget), yields a noisy reward observable only through the one visible assertion, and Weitzman's index gives the optimal open/stop rule when the reward distribution is known. Under KNOWN PROPENSITIES -- which the project already has -- the index is estimable, so this is the theorem to hang our stopping rule on rather than inventing one. Note the savings band, 15-35%, is the same order as ESC on MBPP (~33-44%) and TrACE on a quantized 3B (33-56%): three independent lines converge on 'an optimal stop saves roughly a third of the draws and gains no accuracy'. That convergence is itself the finding.

title: Optimal Bayesian Stopping for Efficient Inference of Consistent LLM Answers
venue_date: arXiv:2602.05395v2, v2 dated 31 May 2026, ICML 2026
what_it_does: Treats mode identification as sequential hypothesis testing: stop at the first n where the posterior probability that the current plurality answer is the true mode exceeds 1-delta. Proves asymptotic optimality of a cheap L=3 aggregated approximation to the exact posterior.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER. Synthetic (Table 1), at confidence 1-delta = 0.8: L=3 needs 6.70 generations versus 7.27 for the prior-free ASC baseline; wall clock 14.2ms (L=3) vs 9.0ms (L=2). Real data (FEval-TTC, Table 2), CommonsenseQA with Qwen-2.5-72B at 1-delta = 0.95: L=3 with an uncertain prior needs 1.00 generation versus 5.28 for ASC. Theorem 3.2, for L >= 3: lim_{delta->0} E[n*,L]/log(1/delta) = 1/((p1-p2) log(p1/p2)), matching the exact-posterior rate.
small_k_evidence: PARTIAL and this is the most relevant formal point: the synthetic comparison sits squarely in our range, 6.70 vs 7.27 generations. But that is synthetic, and the rate constant 1/((p1-p2) log(p1/p2)) blows up as p1 -> p2, i.e. exactly when the top two answer clusters are close -- the regime a weak model lives in. MEASURED-IN-PAPER for the numbers, INFERRED for the degeneracy reading.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- Qwen-2.5-72B, GPT-4o mini, LLaMA-3.1-405B. Nothing under 8B, nothing quantized.
bearing_on_our_decision: Gives us the stopping rule we could actually claim a guarantee for, and it is cheap to implement: a posterior over cluster counts, stop at 1-delta. Two warnings. First, the theorem is about identifying the MODE of the answer distribution, not about identifying a CORRECT answer -- under our strict hidden-test grading those diverge, and H14 shows the mode can be systematically wrong. Second, the stopping time scales as 1/((p1-p2) log(p1/p2)), so on a 3B q4 receiver where the top two execution clusters are nearly tied, the rule will simply never fire inside k=8. Cite it as the formal target and report the empirical p1-p2 distribution from our own draws as the reason it does or does not bind. No code benchmark and no sub-8B model here, so that check is unpublished.

title: MARS: Margin-Adversarial Risk-controlled Stopping for Parallel LLM Test-time Scaling
venue_date: arXiv:2606.12935v1, 11 Jun 2026, preprint (Chen, Li, Liu, Su, Xie)
what_it_does: Stops when the current vote margin over every challenger exceeds the expected adversarial switch damage plus a concentration correction: M_k(t) >= Gamma_k(t) + epsilon(N,delta) for all k. The strongest formal guarantee found for a stopping rule.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER. Guarantee (Corollary 2.5): P(L(T) != L(t) | F_t) <= delta -- the early-stopped answer equals the full-budget vote with probability 1-delta. Savings: 25-47% tokens versus self-consistency, plus a further 14-29% over the DeepConf-Online baseline. Example: Qwen3-next-80B on BRUMO under self-consistency, 47.4% savings at 96.7% accuracy, matching the baseline. Budget: 512 traces (16 warmup + 496 main). Benchmarks: AIME 2025, HMMT, BRUMO 2025, 30 problems each. Models: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-8B, Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-next-80B.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- 512-trace runs only, with a 16-trace warmup that alone exceeds our entire k=8 budget. The paper reports no budget <= 8.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED at our scale -- smallest is DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-8B, unquantized.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the only stopping rule found with a genuine high-probability risk guarantee, and it is the right formal shape for us: it certifies agreement with the full-budget decision, which is exactly the claim a sequential-selection paper under known propensities should be making. But it is unusable as-is -- the warmup alone is 16 traces, double our whole budget -- and the authors state in their own limitations that applicability to other domains such as code generation remains to be validated. That sentence is our opening. The publishable move is a margin-based, risk-controlled stop specialised to k<=8 with execution-cluster margins instead of vote margins, validated on code, which is precisely the cell MARS declines to enter.

title: CITE: Anytime-Valid Statistical Inference in LLM Self-Consistency
venue_date: arXiv:2605.05873v1, 8 May 2026, preprint (Ota, Iwase, Ichihara, Komiyama, Imaizumi)
what_it_does: Builds an e-process / mixture-martingale certificate for self-consistency that controls false certification under ARBITRARY data-dependent stopping, without knowing the set of possible answer labels in advance.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: the guarantee -- provable control of false certification at any prescribed level under arbitrary data-driven stopping, no prior knowledge of the answer category set required; method is an e-process. NOT FOUND: benchmarks, model sizes, sample budgets, certification rates, speedups -- the PDF did not render past the front matter; a 'gpt-oss-2b' reference appears in Appendix H.4 but I could not read the table, so I will not quote it.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED in what I could read. Note the guarantee is budget-free by construction: anytime validity holds at n=3 as well as n=300, which is unusual and in our favour.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED.
bearing_on_our_decision: Methodologically load-bearing for us even though I could not extract its numbers. Our design has a data-dependent stopping rule (draw until the visible assertion passes) AND we want to report inference on the resulting accuracy -- that combination breaks fixed-n CIs, and it is the one statistical hole a reviewer will find in the adaptive-BoN result we already have (paired difference -0.0182, 95% CI [-0.0260,-0.0105]). An e-process gives anytime-valid intervals that survive the optional stopping, at any k, with no large-sample requirement. The fact that its validity does not depend on k is what makes it the right tool for a k<=8 paper. Worth one read of the full PDF before we finalise the analysis plan.

title: S*: Test Time Scaling for Code Generation
venue_date: arXiv:2502.14382 (v1 20 Feb 2025), Findings of EMNLP 2025
what_it_does: Parallel sampling plus iterative debugging plus selection by adaptive input synthesis: an LLM writes inputs that DISTINGUISH candidate pairs, the candidates are executed on them, and the outputs decide. Its ablation is the cleanest published head-to-head of agreement-style selectors for code on small models.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER. LiveCodeBench v2 (511 problems), N=16 samples, temperature 0.7, up to 2 debug rounds, Pass@1: Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct zero-shot 18.4 -> majority vote 25.2 -> self-debugging 27.8 -> S* 42.7. Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct 29.4 -> 40.5 -> 39.9 -> 54.4. GPT-4o-mini 40.9 -> 46.6 -> 51.7 -> 61.3. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B 63.2 -> 68.1 -> 66.2 -> 82.8. Selection ablation (LiveCodeBench v4): Qwen-Coder-7B -- public tests only 42.3, generated tests 42.3, LLM judge 42.3, adaptive input synthesis 44.5; Qwen-Coder-32B -- 54.6 / 57.8 / 55.5 / 58.3; GPT-4o-mini -- 54.1 / 55.2 / 56.3 / 57.3; averages 53.8 / 53.1 / 55.6 / 57.5. The paper's own words on generated-test agreement: no improvement over baseline. Model family spans 0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B/14B/32B. ORACLE / pass@N: NOT FOUND -- I could not retrieve a pass@16 upper bound, so any 'fraction of oracle gap recovered' for S* would be fabricated and I am not reporting one.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- N=16 throughout; no k<=8 ablation retrievable.
small_model_evidence: YES -- Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct at 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B and 7B, i.e. our exact model family one generation back. MEASURED-IN-PAPER. Unquantized.
bearing_on_our_decision: The most directly threatening AND most encouraging result for the selection half. Threatening: majority vote alone lifts the 3B from 18.4 to 25.2 and the 7B from 29.4 to 40.5, so cross-candidate agreement is NOT dead on small coder models. Encouraging: their ablation says agreement against SELF-GENERATED TESTS buys essentially nothing over plain public-test filtering (53.1 vs 53.8 on average; identical 42.3 for the 7B), and what actually works is synthesising inputs chosen to DISTINGUISH candidates (+3.7 average over public tests). That is a sharp design instruction for us: naive execution agreement on arbitrary common inputs is the version the literature already found flat; agreement on inputs selected for discriminative power is the version that wins. Given we hold exactly one visible MBPP assertion, we are in the public-tests-only cell -- the weakest one -- unless we synthesise distinguishing inputs. Also note their big 3B gain confounds selection with 2 rounds of debugging, and our own audit already found adaptive BoN beats a real feedback loop (-0.0182 [-0.0260,-0.0105]), so we should not expect the debugging component to transfer.

title: Semantic Voting: Execution-Grounded Consensus for LLM Code Generation
venue_date: arXiv:2605.08680v1, 9 May 2026, preprint (Jiang, Yi, Zhu; UT Austin)
what_it_does: Execution-consensus clustering on HumanEval+/MBPP+ with an explicit decomposition of the remaining error into GENERATION failures (no correct candidate in the pool) versus SELECTION failures (a correct candidate exists but is not chosen) -- the exact accounting our project needs.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER. HumanEval+ (164 problems), N=50: greedy 93.9 (Pro low); best-of-N 97.0 / 96.3 / 90.9 across Pro-low / Flash-medium / Lite-low; output-pattern majority vote 75.0 / 65.9 / 51.8; weighted voting 98.8 / 96.3 / 92.7; MBR-Exec 97.6 / 95.1 / 92.7; SemanticVote 98.8 / 96.3 / 92.1. MBPP+ (378 problems), N=50: output-pattern MV 77.2 / 51.3 / 39.4; weighted voting 96.8 / 92.3 / 91.5; MBR-Exec 96.8 / 92.3 / 91.3; SemanticVote 97.4 / 91.8 / 90.7. Failure decomposition (Table 5): generation failures average 2.8% (HumanEval+) and 3.9% (MBPP+); SELECTION failures average 1.5-2.7% across all 18 configurations; 0% for SV and WV on Pro-low HumanEval+. Clustering: 1.2-1.5 clusters per problem on average, largest cluster holds 38-48 of 50 candidates. Probe-input sweep D in {5,10,20,30,50} on Flash-medium HumanEval+: 95.1 / 96.3 / 96.3 / 97.0 / 97.0, saturating at D>=30, clusters per problem rising only 1.20 -> 1.43. Bootstrap: SemanticVote vs weighted voting differs by -0.79 to +0.61 pp, p>0.05 in all 18 configurations; execution-based vs output-pattern MV differs by 18-52 pp. Models: Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite (preview).
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- N=50 primary, N=100 in ablations. The D-sweep varies the number of PROBE INPUTS down to 5, not the number of candidates.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- frontier Gemini preview models only, sizes undisclosed. The weakest receiver (Flash Lite) still scores 90.9 best-of-50 on HumanEval+.
bearing_on_our_decision: Four transferable lessons plus one warning. (1) Our failure decomposition has a published precedent and vocabulary -- use generation vs selection failure, and note that for frontier models selection failure is already down to 1.5-2.7%, which is why nobody has bothered with the small-model case. (2) Output-pattern agreement is catastrophic: 51.8-77.2 against 90.9-93.9 greedy, i.e. voting on raw text is 18-52 pp WORSE than execution grounding. Our agreement must be on execution outputs, never on code strings. (3) Which execution aggregator we pick does not matter (p>0.05, within 1.4 pp across 18 configs) -- so we should not burn our 909-calls-per-hour budget comparing MBR-Exec against weighted voting against cluster-size. (4) Probe inputs saturate by D=30 and 5 already gets within 1.9 pp, so the input-generation cost is bounded. The warning: their clusters are nearly degenerate (1.2-1.5 per problem, largest holding 38-48 of 50) because their models are strong and agree. On our 3B q4 receiver clusters will fragment, and with k=8 draws a fragmented execution signature space may leave the largest cluster at size 2 -- a coin flip. Measuring the cluster-size distribution on our existing 3-4 draw logs is a zero-new-compute go/no-go test, and it should be done before committing any of the 4,488 calls.

title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
venue_date: arXiv:2408.03314, 6 Aug 2024, preprint (Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar); not confirmed as an ICLR 2025 publication on the arXiv landing page
what_it_does: The reference point for compute-optimal test-time scaling: allocate revision-versus-search and per-question budget as a function of estimated difficulty, rather than uniformly.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: difficulty-aware compute-optimal allocation matches best-of-N using up to 4x less test-time compute, given explicitly as 16 versus 64 generations. Generation budgets swept 4 to 256, with headline comparisons at 4, 16, 64, 256. Model: PaLM 2-S* on MATH (12k train, 500 test). FLOPs-matched: the smaller model with compute-optimal test-time allocation beats a ~14x larger pretrained model without extra test-time compute on easy and intermediate questions, but underperforms on the hardest problems, depending on the inference-to-pretraining token ratio. At the lowest budgets (4-16) the paper reports significant early improvements from compute-optimal scaling but, as far as I could extract, no precise numerical deltas at those budgets -- NOT FOUND.
small_k_evidence: WEAK -- budget 4 and 16 appear in the sweep, but the 4x claim is 16-vs-64 and the small-budget deltas are not tabulated in what I could read.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- PaLM 2-S* parameter count is undisclosed, and no open sub-8B model appears.
bearing_on_our_decision: Background and framing, not evidence for us. Its two load-bearing assets are unavailable to us: a trained process/outcome verifier, and a difficulty estimator built from a large labelled train split. Its most relevant sentence is the negative one -- the small-model-plus-test-time-compute advantage holds on easy and intermediate questions and FAILS on the hardest, which is exactly the shape of our 230-task informative band versus the tail. Cite for the 16-vs-64 4x figure and for the honest caveat that the entire compute-optimal literature is built at budgets 2-32x ours on an undisclosed proprietary model.

title: When Self-Consistency Backfires: Majority Vote Hurts the Majority of Hard Science Problems for Small LLMs
venue_date: arXiv:2608.11403v2, 15 Aug 2026; v1 accepted at the COLM 2026 Workshop on Efficient Reasoning
what_it_does: Pre-registered test of whether agreement-based aggregation helps small instruct models on hard problems, with an exploratory/confirmatory split. Finds it hurts per-problem accuracy on the majority of problems even while lifting the aggregate.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-Turbo and Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Lite on GPQA Diamond (198 questions), N=64: backfire rate (majority vote lowers per-problem accuracy) 56.6% of problems for Qwen and 65.7% for Llama; single-sample accuracy 0.342 / 0.273; 64-sample majority vote 0.369 / 0.313; worst single problem -47 and -46 points. Calibration: in the HIGHEST-agreement bin Qwen's plurality is correct only 52.5% of the time and Llama's only 28.6% -- lower than Llama's own LOW-agreement bin, i.e. the agreement-correctness relationship is inverted for the weaker model. Mean token entropy predicts backfire with AUC 0.631 (Qwen) and 0.523 (Llama), the latter essentially chance. Design: effect observed on 47 exploratory problems, pre-registered and confirmed on a 151-problem split, all four confirmatory hypotheses passed.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- N=64. INFERRED: the mechanism is strictly worse at small k, since a fragmented plurality at k=8 is decided by one or two draws.
small_model_evidence: YES -- Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, the same family and size as one of our two receivers, plus Llama-3-8B. MEASURED-IN-PAPER, though hosted/unquantized variants.
bearing_on_our_decision: The most important cautionary result in this search and the one that most directly explains our own nulls. On a Qwen2.5-7B-class receiver, agreement is nearly uninformative about correctness (highest-agreement bin only 52.5% correct; entropy AUC 0.523-0.631). That is the same phenomenon as our cheap-feature models recovering -0.18, -0.06, 0.00, 0.00 of the gap with all intervals covering zero: on weak receivers, confidence-like signals do not carry correctness. It also warns that an aggregate improvement can hide per-problem harm on the majority of problems, so our analysis must report the paired per-task distribution, not just the mean -- which our 230-task informative band and paired-difference machinery already support. Crucially, the failing signal here is TEXTUAL/probabilistic agreement. Execution agreement is a different, grounded signal, and H12's 18-52 pp gap between execution-based and output-pattern voting is exactly the reason to expect the two to diverge. Our study is the one that separates them at small k on a weak receiver.

title: Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
venue_date: arXiv:2508.15260v1, 21 Aug 2025, preprint (Fu, Wang, Tian, Zhao; Meta AI / UCSD)
what_it_does: Online trace-level early termination on internal confidence: warm up with 16 traces, set a stopping threshold at a percentile of warmup confidence, kill any trace whose running group confidence drops below it, and stop generating once consensus reaches tau=0.95 or the budget runs out.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER. Budget B=512 primary, swept over {32,64,128,256,512}. N_init=16 warmup; DeepConf-low retention eta=10% (90th-percentile threshold), DeepConf-high eta=90%. GPT-OSS-120B on AIME 2025: 84.7% token reduction with accuracy rising 97.1 -> 97.9. DeepSeek-8B AIME24: majority@512 86.7%, DeepConf-high -59.0% tokens, DeepConf-low -77.9% tokens at 92.5% accuracy; AIME25: majority@512 82.3%, -40.9% and -69.0% tokens at 86.4%. Overall DeepConf-low spans 43% to 84.7% token reduction. No formal guarantee -- the authors only observe accuracy approaching offline accuracy as N_init grows. Models: DeepSeek-8B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B, GPT-OSS-20B, GPT-OSS-120B.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED, and structurally impossible here -- the warmup alone is 16 traces, twice our entire budget. Smallest budget shown is B=32.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- nothing under 8B, nothing quantized. No code benchmark either; math and GPQA only.
bearing_on_our_decision: The current strongest-savings stopping method, and it is out of reach for us on two counts: it needs token-level internal confidence (available in principle through llama.cpp logprobs, but noisy under q4_k_m) and it needs a 16-trace warmup we cannot afford. Its real value to us is as the reference for how large savings get when budget is unconstrained -- 43-84.7% -- which bounds what our k=8 rule can claim and makes clear that the interesting contribution at k=8 cannot be savings magnitude. It also confirms the pattern across the whole angle: every high-savings method buys compute, not accuracy (97.1 -> 97.9 is within noise on 30 problems).

title: Make Every Penny Count: Difficulty-Adaptive Self-Consistency (DSC)
venue_date: arXiv:2408.13457v2, v2 dated 24 Jan 2025, preprint (Wang, Feng, Li, Yuan, Zhang, Pan, Wang, Hu, Li)
what_it_does: Pre-allocates per-question sample budgets from an LLM-produced difficulty RANKING (rank problems, split easy/hard, give easy problems one sample, predict counts for hard ones from difficulty neighbours) instead of reacting to observed agreement.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: average cost reduction 65.29% versus SC and 24.81% versus ESC on GPT-4; 56.04% versus SC and 21.86% versus ESC on GPT-3.5-Turbo, at comparable accuracy, across MATH, GSM8K, CommonsenseQA, StrategyQA, Letter Concatenation and Coin Flip. Max sample sizes swept 16-48. Only ~3.8% of questions (GPT-4) benefit at all from multiple sampling versus a single chain. Models: GPT-4, GPT-3.5-Turbo, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 in Appendix A.2.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- max sample sweep starts at 16.
small_model_evidence: PARTIAL -- Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 appears in an appendix; no main-table numbers for it and nothing under 7B.
bearing_on_our_decision: Its methodological point matters more than its numbers: DSC beats ESC not by a smarter stop but by spending nothing on questions that do not need draws, and it reports that only ~3.8% of GPT-4 questions benefit from extra sampling at all. That is the same insight our audit reached by construction when it isolated a 230-task informative band out of 561, and it tells us where the remaining compute win lives: allocation across tasks, not stopping within a task. It also underlines that the whole DSC/ASC/ESC family is evaluated at budgets 16-48 with zero code benchmarks, so none of its cost numbers transfer to k=8 on MBPP.

title: Reliability-Aware Adaptive Self-Consistency (ReASC)
venue_date: arXiv:2601.02970 (submitted 6 Jan 2026, revised 20 Apr 2026), ACL 2026
what_it_does: Two-stage rule: answer confidently-answerable instances from a single sample, then accumulate remaining samples weighting response frequency by a confidence score rather than counting votes.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: reduces inference cost by up to 70% relative to self-consistency while preserving accuracy on GSM8K. Models include Gemma-3-4B-it plus models up to 27B. Benchmarks: GSM8K and three others. NOT FOUND: the max sample budget, average samples consumed, and the head-to-head deltas against ASC and ESC -- the landing page does not carry the tables.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED.
small_model_evidence: PARTIAL -- Gemma-3-4B-it is under 8B. MEASURED-IN-PAPER that it is included; its per-model numbers NOT FOUND.
bearing_on_our_decision: Peer-reviewed confirmation that the frequency-plus-confidence weighting beats plain vote counting, which is the same direction as H12's weighted voting result. Weak evidence for us: no code benchmark, and the budget regime is unreported. Its 'single sample for confident instances' stage is, however, the cheapest possible version of the allocation rule that H6 and H16 both endorse, and it is trivially implementable on top of our visible-assertion verdict -- if the one visible assertion passes on draw 1, stop. We already measure that rule at 0.7455.

title: The Larger the Better? Improved LLM Code-Generation via Budget Reallocation
venue_date: arXiv:2404.00725v2, v2 dated 25 Jul 2024, preprint (Hassid, Remez, Gehring, Schwartz, Adi)
what_it_does: Fixes a wall-clock budget and asks whether a small model drawing many samples beats a large model drawing one, on code, with unit-test selection.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: a 7B/13B model generating multiple outputs beats a 70B model generating one by up to 15 points on HumanEval and MBPP; on the APPS competition split the 13B beats the 70B by ~5 points under wall-time constraints; the 13B matches the 70B using one quarter of the time. Sample counts n = 2000/1000/400/200 for 7B/13B/34B/70B. Selection is by unit-test execution (pass@k), which the paper itself frames as an idealised ceiling; it states that when unit tests are unavailable, ranking-based selection falls short of the larger model.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- n in the hundreds to thousands.
small_model_evidence: YES for size (7B, 13B) but unquantized and the code-specialised Code Llama family; the comparison of interest is against a 70B, not within the sub-8B band.
bearing_on_our_decision: Establishes that our premise -- spend compute on many draws from a small model rather than on a bigger model -- is a published, code-specific result, which is useful for our framing given we have no cluster and no API budget. But it also states our central difficulty in the authors' own words: the 15-point win is measured with unit-test selection, i.e. close to oracle, and WITHOUT unit tests ranking-based selection falls short. Our hidden-test protocol with exactly one visible MBPP assertion is the no-unit-tests regime. So this paper is simultaneously the best argument that the oracle gap is worth chasing and the clearest statement that nobody has shown how to convert it without the tests.

title: Self-Consistency Is Losing Its Edge: Diminishing Returns and Rising Costs in Modern LLMs
venue_date: arXiv:2511.00751v2, 28 Oct 2025, preprint (Chiyan Loo, single author)
what_it_does: Measures what self-consistency actually buys on current models across sample counts 3, 5, 10, 15, 20 and charges the token cost.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: HotpotQA with Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, only 0.4 points between single-CoT and the 20-sample configuration -- roughly a 20x token increase for 0.4 points. MATH-500 with Flash-Lite, 1.6 points across sampled paths; MATH-500 with Gemini-2.5-Pro, 1.6 points (98.0 -> 99.6 at 15 paths), about 15x compute for 1.6 points. Flash-Lite on MATH-500 peaks around 10 samples and declines slightly beyond 15; HotpotQA gains fluctuate irregularly rather than improving monotonically. Sample counts tested: 3, 5, 10, 15, 20. The majority-vote versus oracle pass@k gap is not discussed.
small_k_evidence: YES for the sweep -- k = 3 and 5 are included, which is our existing log regime. MEASURED-IN-PAPER, though the accuracy differences at those k are within the reported noise.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- frontier Gemini models only, no sub-8B, no code benchmark.
bearing_on_our_decision: Single-author preprint with a small experimental base, so weight it lightly, but it is the one paper that sweeps k down to 3 and 5 and reports the honest answer: agreement-based aggregation is worth fractions of a point on strong models and can go non-monotone. It supports the framing that the interesting version of our question is NOT 'does agreement voting help' -- on strong models it is nearly exhausted, on weak models H14 shows it can invert -- but 'does EXECUTION agreement, which is a different and grounded signal, help a weak receiver at k<=8 where the oracle gap is still 7.4 points'. That question is unanswered in the literature.

title: Surprisal-Guided Selection: Compute-Optimal Test-Time Strategies for Execution-Grounded Code Generation
venue_date: arXiv:2602.07670v1, 7 Feb 2026, preprint (Jarrod Barnes, Arc Intelligence)
what_it_does: Uses model surprisal to decide which candidates to spend execution budget on, in an execution-grounded code setting, and compares against oracle selection.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: GPT-OSS-120B with LoRA rank 16, KernelBench L1 (20 eval tasks, 80 training), 320 total rollouts across 5 tasks per evaluation, temperature 0.25, max 1024 tokens. Table 3 at K=64 (Subset 1): best-correct oracle 100% fast_1 at 226.9x mean speedup; surprisal-guided-top3 100% at 139.0x; surprisal-guided 80% at 41.2x; random-correct 59.2% at 30.0x; confidence-guided 50% at 11.6x. Pass@K scaling: K=1 53.3%, K=4 89.5%, K=16 99.9%, K=64 100%. Best-of-N at K=64 reaches 90% on the full 20-task eval; test-time-training best-of-adaptation only 30.6%. Surprisal-guided beats confidence-guided by 30 points.
small_k_evidence: PARTIAL -- pass@4 is reported (89.5% vs 53.3% at K=1), but every selection result is at K=64. No selection numbers at K<=8.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- a single 120B model. The authors report nothing under 8B and no budget <=8.
bearing_on_our_decision: Two useful transfers and one warning. Useful: it shows a surprisal signal beating a confidence signal by 30 points for execution-grounded code selection, which suggests that if we do try a cheap model-internal signal, per-token surprisal is the better bet than sequence confidence -- and llama.cpp gives us logprobs. It also reports a very large oracle-versus-selected gap (100% vs 80%) that selection only partly closes even on a 120B. Warning: n=20 eval tasks on GPU-kernel generation with a speedup metric is about as far from 561 audited MBPP/HumanEval tasks with hidden-assertion grading as an execution-grounded code paper can get, so treat it as a hypothesis source, not evidence.

title: Natural Language to Code Translation with Execution (MBR-EXEC)
what_it_does: The original execution-agreement selector for code: execute each candidate on a small set of test inputs, treat identical output signatures as semantic equivalence, and pick the minimum-Bayes-risk candidate under that equivalence. This IS the method our project calls 'cross-candidate execution agreement'.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER at the abstract level only: execution and simulated execution significantly outperform execution-unaware selection, and MBR-EXEC consistently improves over execution-unaware baselines across datasets. NOT FOUND: model sizes, per-dataset accuracies, oracle comparisons, the sample counts n, and any accuracy-versus-n curve. Both the arXiv landing page and the ACL Anthology page carry only the abstract, and the PDF did not render for extraction. I am not quoting numbers I could not read. For a current, fully-tabulated evaluation of MBR-Exec see H12: HumanEval+ N=50 gives 97.6 / 95.1 / 92.7 and MBPP+ gives 96.8 / 92.3 / 91.3, statistically indistinguishable from the newer aggregators (p>0.05, within 1.4 pp).
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED in retrievable form.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED -- 2022-era Codex models, sizes undisclosed.
bearing_on_our_decision: Establishes priority: the method we are calling 'the obvious untested candidate' is four years old and named. Our contribution therefore cannot be the method -- it must be the REGIME (k<=8, sub-8B quantized receiver, exactly one visible assertion, hidden-test grading, 561 audited tasks, paired intervals) and the DECISION (does it recover the measured 0.0737 / 0.0351 gap, yes or no, with a CI). H12's finding that MBR-Exec is statistically indistinguishable from every newer execution aggregator means we should implement the 2022 method and not spend our 909-calls-per-hour budget on aggregator variants.

title: Selection Without Signal, Recovery Through Expression: A Measurement Study of Post-Hoc Falsification Operators for Frozen Small Code Models
venue_date: arXiv:2606.16999v1 [cs.SE], 15 June 2026 (Mehmet İşcan, PythaLab / Yıldız Technical University). Preprint, no venue stated.
what_it_does: Near-exact methodological twin of this project, one model scale down. Generates pools ONCE at k=8, T=0.8 from three frozen local small code models (Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B, Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B, run on a single 6GB consumer GPU, UNQUANTIZED), and evaluates 26 post-hoc operators -- including execution-consensus (MBR-Exec-style: cluster public-passers by execution fingerprint, take the modal cluster) -- against a Best-of-N baseline defined EXACTLY as ours: 'draw k candidates, return the first that passes the visible tests'. Leakage-free protocol, hidden execution oracle, paired McNemar. Replicated on HumanEval+ (164) and MBPP+ (370, built from MBPP-sanitized).
key_numbers:

- HumanEval+ DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B: 29 / 29 / 29 / headroom 0 (b10=0,b01=0)

MEASURED-IN-PAPER, 'capability scissors': on 255 visible-passing candidates from Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B, a wavelet/embedding probe scores AUC 0.479 for HIDDEN correctness (delta-AUC vs embedding -0.004, p=0.60), while the SAME features predict public-pass at AUC 0.985.
MEASURED-IN-PAPER, 'coverage wall': deepening to k=16 on 30 held-out hard tasks, 16/30 still have NO hidden-correct candidate; 11/30 were already covered at k=8 (so loss was selection not coverage); only 3/30 gain a hidden-correct candidate, of which just 1 gains a VISIBLE-PASSING one a leakage-free selector could grab.
MEASURED-IN-PAPER, 'consensus trap' (defined as: public-passing majority hidden-wrong AND some candidate hidden-correct): on two purpose-built trap benchmarks the model emitted the triggering bug on 0/10 and 2/16 tasks, never as the consensus majority; ~83% of the model's real bugs are invisible to any sound metamorphic relation.
MEASURED-IN-PAPER, stopping: adaptive consensus early-stop (ACE) saves ~19% of samples at a zero-harm operating point (b10=0, Hoeffding-Bentkus Learn-then-Test); the aggressive ~64% saving incurs b10=2 regressions. On the weak model the saving collapses to ~7-12%.
MEASURED-IN-PAPER, Proposition 1: a distribution-free do-no-harm certificate cannot bound population harm at <=alpha even at ZERO observed harm unless n >= ceil(log delta / log(1-alpha)) = 45 at alpha=0.05, delta=0.10.
small_k_evidence: This is the ONLY paper found that runs at exactly k=8. All of Table 6 is k=8. The k=16 deepening experiment is the only larger-k point and it shows coverage does not grow.
small_model_evidence: Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B, Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B -- all far under 8B, all run locally on a 6GB consumer GPU. NOT quantized (paper explicitly says 0.5-1.5B 'run without quantization'). No 3B or 7B cell, and no quantized cell.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the paper that decides the question, and it decides it against the execution-agreement hypothesis. It runs OUR method, at OUR k, against OUR exact baseline, on OUR benchmarks (MBPP-sanitized via MBPP+, plus HumanEval), with a hidden-test oracle, and finds execution-fingerprint clustering captures 14% of the headroom pooled and is significant in ZERO of six cells. Its 'capability scissors' result (AUC 0.479 for hidden correctness vs 0.985 for public-pass, on visible-passers) is an independent replication of our own negative audit (GBM/logistic fractions recovered -0.18, -0.06, 0.00, 0.00, all intervals covering zero) -- same phenomenon, different features, different model family. Its 'consensus trap' lemma explains WHY: a leakage-free selector can only net-gain on tasks where the visible-passing majority is hidden-wrong AND a hidden-correct candidate is in the pool, and that mass is measured near zero. Three things are NOT covered and are our only remaining daylight: (1) no 3B/7B cell -- their headroom rates are 4.3-4.6pp while our 3B gap is 7.37pp, ~60-70% larger, so our trap mass may be genuinely bigger; (2) no quantized/llama.cpp cell -- q4_k_m may inject the extra incoherent-error mass that refills the trap; (3) their visible filter is the full EvalPlus/public test set, not a single assertion, and they explicitly predict 'a WEAKER visible-test filter (so that visible-passing, hidden-wrong majorities become common) would refill the consensus trap' -- our strict one-assertion-visible MBPP split IS that weaker filter. That sentence is the strongest pro-project statement in the whole literature, and it is a prediction, not a measurement. Also note their ACE result is a ready-made baseline for the STOPPING half of the project, and their Proposition 1 (n>=45 for a do-no-harm certificate) is a design constraint we should adopt.

- Qwen2.5-Coder-32B: 54.6 | 57.8 | 55.5 | 58.3

NOT REPORTED: per-model pass@N (oracle coverage) at N=16 on LiveCodeBench v2, so the fraction of the ORACLE gap that Majority Vote/execution clustering closes CANNOT be computed. Figure 4 (right) plots Pass@N vs N in {1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128} but gives no numeric values in text.
small_k_evidence: YES, and this is the crucial one: Table 3 is at N=8. At N=8 on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, three separate cheap selectors on top of public-test filtering -- generated tests, LLM judge, and (implicitly, since Public Only already filters) plain agreement -- all recovered EXACTLY ZERO (42.3 / 42.3 / 42.3). Only Adaptive Input Synthesis, which calls GPT-4o-mini to synthesize a maximally-distinguishing input, got +2.2. Averaged over the four models, Generated Tests was NEGATIVE vs Public Only (53.1 vs 53.8).
small_model_evidence: YES, and it is the closest model match in the whole literature: Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct at 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B -- the same family and the same two sizes as our receivers. No quantization: all experiments are full-precision on H100s. Also note the N=16 gains SHRINK monotonically with model size going down: +11.1 at 7B, +6.8 at 3B, +4.0 at 1.5B, +1.3 at 0.5B.
bearing_on_our_decision: Two opposite-signed readings and we must hold both. Positive: at N=16, execution-result clustering on Qwen2.5-Coder-3B gives +6.8pp and on 7B gives +11.1pp -- larger in absolute terms than our entire selection gap (7.37pp on 3B, 3.51pp on 7B). That is the single most encouraging number for the project, and it is on our exact model family. Negative, and more load-bearing: their N=16 gains are measured against ZERO-SHOT pass@1, not against a visible-test filter. Table 3, which IS measured against a public-test filter and IS at N=8, shows cheap selectors recovering 0.0pp on the 7B. Our 0.7455 baseline is already a visible-test filter, so Table 3 is our comparison, not Table 1, and Table 3 says nothing cheap works at N=8 on a 7B Qwen. The one thing that did work (+2.2pp) needs a stronger external model (GPT-4o-mini) to synthesize distinguishing inputs -- which we do not have budget for, and which is also how they generated the clustering inputs in Table 1, a confound that inflates the Table 1 numbers relative to what we could reproduce locally. Also: their benchmark is LiveCodeBench, much harder than MBPP/HumanEval, where the pool is more diverse and clustering has more to bite on. Actionable: Adaptive Input Synthesis at N=8 is the ONE published selector that beat a public-test filter on a 7B model, at +2.2pp -- if we test anything beyond plain clustering, test a cheap local imitation of that.

There is NO ablation varying n; Table 4 holds n=100 fixed and varies only the test-case count. So nothing here tells us what clustering does when the pool is 8. All of our k=10 fractions above are UPPER BOUNDS on what our regime could get, because 100 draws give clustering far more signal than 8.
small_model_evidence: One model under 8B: INCODER-6B. It is the WORST cell for clustering alone -- AlphaCode-C recovers only 10.9% of the k=10 HumanEval gap and 21.4% on MBPP, and only 4.2% / 12.0% of the k=100 gap. CODEGEN-MONO-16B, the other weak open model, goes outright NEGATIVE with clustering alone on both benchmarks. No quantized models. No 3B model.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the closest thing to a direct estimate of the project's proposed method's ceiling, and the estimate is poor. AlphaCode-C -- run every candidate on common inputs, prefer the largest output-agreement cluster, which is verbatim our plan -- recovers only 4-18% of the full oracle gap and 11-29% of the k=10 gap, WITH a 100-sample pool, and it goes NEGATIVE on the weaker of the two open models. The two open, non-API models (INCODER-6B, CODEGEN-16B) are the worst two cells in the table, which is the wrong direction for a 3B/7B q4_k_m receiver. Scaling our own numbers: 21% of our 3B gap of 0.0737 is 0.0155, roughly 7 tasks out of 448, which our own audit's interval widths will not separate from zero; on the 7B (gap 0.0351) it is 0.0074, about 3 tasks -- unmeasurable. Two further points cut against us. First, the gap between AlphaCode-C and full CodeT shows that most of the recoverable signal is in MODEL-GENERATED TESTS (having expected outputs), not in cross-candidate agreement -- and generating tests costs receiver calls we cannot afford at 909 calls/hour. Second and most directly: CodeT explicitly REMOVED the example assertions from all problem contexts, and Appendix B reports that leaving them in makes CodeT pass@1 NEGATIVE by up to -4.2%. Our design keeps exactly one assertion visible. So the single published measurement of this method family in a regime with a visible example assertion is a negative number.

bearing_on_our_decision: Two findings here are decisive and one is the best pro-project evidence we have. (1) Their headline -- 'once candidates are executed on diverse inputs, the aggregation rule has limited effect: SEMANTICVOTE, weighted voting and MBR-Exec are statistically indistinguishable across all 18 configurations' -- means there is no clever variant of output clustering to invent. If plain largest-cluster does not work for us, neither will a weighted or MBR variant. That collapses a whole branch of our design space to one arm. (2) On MBPP+ their clustering is 0.32pp WORSE on average than simply returning the first syntactically valid candidate, capturing -13% of the BoN-to-oracle headroom; combined with Table 5's finding that selection failure is only 2.5-2.7pp of a 3.9pp gap, this is a second independent 'clustering adds nothing over a cheap filter' result. (3) The pro-project finding, and it is sharp: their Table 1 ablation shows the INPUT SOURCE is the dominant lever (up to 11.3pp), and their EXAMPLE-ONLY row -- using only the 1-3 example inputs from the problem description, which is OUR regime with exactly one visible MBPP assertion -- is the WORST or second-worst strategy in every column, costing 6-11pp versus LLM-generated inputs. This is the only paper that directly measures the 'only the given example inputs are available' case, and it measures it as the failure mode. The implication for us is unambiguous: if we run the execution-agreement arm using only the one visible assertion's input, we are running the weakest published configuration of the weakest published lever. Any honest version of this arm must budget receiver calls for generating additional distinguishing inputs -- which at 909 calls/hour on one M5 has to come out of the 8-draw budget.

title: Natural Language to Code Translation with Execution (MBR-EXEC)

Sample k programs, execute each on a small number of test INPUTS (outputs not needed), and pick the program whose execution results have minimum Bayes risk against the others -- i.e. the largest output-agreement cluster's representative. This is the closest published method to the project's proposal, and it is the only one that uses the DATASET'S OWN example assertion as the execution input rather than model-generated tests.

MEASURED-IN-PAPER, Table 2, code-davinci-001, 25 samples per method (5 prompts x 3-shot, T=0.3):

- Spider: Greedy 50.8, Sample 48.5, MBR-EXEC 63.6 +/- 0.8
- NL2Bash: Greedy 52.8, Sample 53.0, MBR-EXEC 58.5 +/- 0.3

Figures 2, 6 and 7 all sweep sample size from small to ~120, and Figure 7 overlays MBR-EXEC against ExPass@K (the oracle) on the same axis, so the small-k end of the curve EXISTS -- but no numeric values are printed and the text gives none. The paper says only that returns diminish beyond roughly 25-30 samples. If we need the k=8 point, it has to come from re-reading the figure at high zoom or from the authors' released code, not from the text.

bearing_on_our_decision: This is the one paper whose SIGNAL is the same as ours: it uses the dataset's own single example assertion as the execution input, executes candidates on it, and clusters by output -- no model-generated tests, no stronger helper model, no hidden-test leakage. That makes its +10.5pp on MBPP (47.7 -> 58.2 at k=25) the most transferable published number for our arm, and roughly 38% of the oracle gap by my figure-read. But three discounts apply and they are large. First, its baseline is RANDOM sampling, not 'first candidate whose visible assertion passes' -- our 0.7455 baseline already banks a large part of what MBR-EXEC's +10.5pp represents, because their selector and our baseline are reading the same single assertion. Second, k=25 not 8, and the paper's own Figure 6 shows the one-input configuration is dominated by the three-input configuration at every sample size -- we have exactly one input available on MBPP, so we sit on the lower curve. Third, code-davinci-001 is a strong model; nothing here speaks to a q4_k_m 3B. Net: this paper establishes that the mechanism is real and that one visible assertion is enough to make it work at all, which is more than CodeT or Semantic Voting concede. It does not establish that it survives k=8, a weak quantized receiver, or a baseline that already filters on that same assertion.
