(2) Its Figure 5 is the single most valuable unretrieved data point in this whole search -- it is the only published sweep of an agreement-clustering method down to 2 solutions, and the text claims the gain survives there. Before committing 22 contended hours of M5 time, it is worth 30 minutes to read that figure at the k=8 tick, or to run their released code on our pools. The counterweight: SRank requires 100 generated TEST SEQUENCES per problem in addition to the 100 solutions, so its per-task receiver cost is far beyond our 909 calls/hour budget, and it reports no oracle, so even its huge absolute gains cannot be converted into the fraction-of-gap number our decision needs.

title: Competition-Level Code Generation with AlphaCode
venue_date: arXiv:2203.07814, 8 Feb 2022; Science 378(6624):1092-1097, Dec 2022. Li, Choi, Chung, Kushman, Schrittwieser, Leblond et al. (DeepMind).
what_it_does: The origin of clustering-by-program-behaviour. Filters samples by the example tests in the problem statement, then clusters the survivors by their behaviour on MODEL-GENERATED test inputs (programs with the same output on each generated input go in one cluster), then submits one representative per cluster in descending cluster-size order. Evaluated with the n@k metric on CodeContests.
key_numbers:
MEASURED-IN-PAPER: around 100,000 (up to ~1 million) solutions generated PER PROBLEM; filtering on the example tests removes MORE THAN 99% of samples (less than 1% of samples pass the example tests); clustering then selects the top 10 for submission, giving 10@k performance in the top 54% of Codeforces participants.
MEASURED-IN-PAPER, Figure 3D: 10@k solve rate vs different sample-selection methods -- clustering plus filtering improves the solve rate as more samples are taken; the benefit of clustering over random selection among filtered samples GROWS with k.
NOT REPORTED: MBPP. NOT REPORTED: HumanEval. NOT REPORTED: any k<=10 point (the entire study lives at k in the tens of thousands to millions). NOT REPORTED: any model under 8B (AlphaCode is 300M-41B encoder-decoder, and the headline result is the 41B). NOT REPORTED: pass@1 / oracle gap on our benchmarks.
small_k_evidence: EXPLICITLY ABSENT, and that absence is the finding. The method is designed for, and only validated at, k of order 10^5. Its own mechanism requires it: with fewer than 1% of samples surviving the example-test filter, a pool of 8 draws yields 0 survivors in expectation on CodeContests-difficulty tasks, so there is nothing to cluster. The clustering benefit in Figure 3D is reported as INCREASING in k, i.e. smallest exactly where we are.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED. No model under 8B, no quantized model, no MBPP/HumanEval evaluation at all.
bearing_on_our_decision: AlphaCode is cited as the ancestor of our proposed method but provides ZERO evidence for our regime, and its scaling shape argues against it. Its clustering is a device for compressing 10^5 filtered candidates into 10 submissions -- a fundamentally different problem from choosing 1 of 8. With 8 draws there are at most 8 clusters and typically far fewer: Semantic Voting MEASURES 1.2-1.5 clusters per problem on average on MBPP with N=50 candidates, with the largest cluster holding 38-48 of the 50. Extrapolated to k=8 that is often a single cluster containing every candidate, which makes largest-cluster selection degenerate to 'return an arbitrary candidate' -- i.e. identical to our existing 0.7455 baseline. That degeneracy, not any modelling subtlety, is the mechanical reason to expect near-zero recovery at k=8, and it is the same mechanism İşcan's 'near-empty consensus trap' measures directly. When writing this up, do NOT cite AlphaCode as support for clustering at k=8; cite it as the reason to expect clustering to be vacuous at k=8.

bearing_on_our_decision: Two reasons it does not rescue us and one reason to keep it on file. (1) Its test inputs are GENERATED BY GPT-4o. Every number above is an execution-agreement method being fed distinguishing inputs by a frontier model. We have no API budget, so the honest local analogue is either the single visible assertion (Semantic Voting's worst configuration) or receiver-generated inputs paid for out of our 909 calls/hour. The published margins are not transferable. (2) No oracle is reported and no k ablation exists, so this paper cannot answer either of our two questions (what fraction of the gap, at what k). Its HumanEval 'Original' column (Codex 38.7, StarCoder 37.6) is also far below those models' usual pass@1 and I could not verify from the text whether it is a single temperature-sampled draw or something else -- treat the absolute HumanEval deltas with suspicion; the MBPP-sanitized table is the more trustworthy one and there the margins over CodeT are a modest +0.3 to +4.9pp. (3) Worth keeping: its ablation says MEMBERSHIP queries (does this candidate pass this test) carry 24.6% and EQUIVALENCE queries (do these two candidates agree) only 7.7%. If that ratio holds at k=8, it says the signal is overwhelmingly in 'does it pass a test' -- which our 0.7455 visible-assertion baseline already extracts -- and only marginally in 'do candidates agree with each other', which is precisely the extra thing execution-agreement clustering would buy us. That is a third independent line pointing the same way.

title: Confidence-Gated Transductive Test Generation for Code Reranking (CoTT)
venue_date: arXiv:2609.12489v1, 11 Sep 2026. Sungjae Lee, Youngsik Yoon, Seockbean Song, Siwei Wang, Wei Chen, Jungseul Ok. cs.AI.
what_it_does: The most recent work in the family (nine days before today). Reranks code candidates using transductive test generation gated by 'inductive confidence', where the inductive confidence is computed by AGREEMENT OR MAJORITY VOTING among sampled programs -- i.e. it uses execution agreement as a confidence signal and only pays for test generation when agreement is low. 20 inductive samples and 10 transductive samples per call. Evaluated on HumanEval-R+ and MBPP-R+ reranking datasets, where each task is paired with FIVE candidate solutions of varying correctness.

MEASURED-IN-PAPER, Table 1, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, HumanEval-R+ / MBPP-R+ [Top-1 | Bottom-1 | Spearman rho | cost]:
- CoTT (proposed) 62.5/61.6 | 66.7/58.7 | 0.650/0.580 | $0.065
- TT without gating 63.1/58.5 | 66.2/56.1 | 0.676/0.576 | $0.077
- rStar-Coder 59.8/59.8 | 65.4/58.1 | 0.611/0.559 | $0.058
- SYNTRA 56.6/51.8 | 59.8/56.7 | 0.585/0.539 | $0.069
MEASURED-IN-PAPER: five candidate solutions per task.
NOT REPORTED: oracle performance, and therefore NO fraction of the oracle gap. The paper does not quantify gap closure and provides no ground-truth-test execution baseline.
NOT REPORTED: any model other than Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. No quantized models. No visible/hidden single-assertion split.
small_k_evidence: YES on pool size -- five candidates per task, the smallest k in anything found, closer to our 3-4 existing log draws than to our planned 8. But it is a RERANKING benchmark with candidates supplied by the dataset, not a generate-then-select experiment, and the confidence signal itself consumes 20 inductive plus 10 transductive samples per call, so its true compute footprint is much larger than k=5.
small_model_evidence: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct only -- at 8B, just above our 7B, and NOT quantized. Nothing at 3B. The paper reports dollar costs ($0.058-$0.077 per task), implying API serving, not local llama.cpp.
bearing_on_our_decision: Two useful signals, no decisive number. First, it independently confirms that the CURRENT frontier of this literature uses execution agreement as a GATE on when to spend compute rather than as the selector itself -- which is exactly the shape of the project's surviving question (when to stop spending compute) and a strong hint that the stopping half is the more defensible half. Second, its most telling number is negative for gating: ungated transductive test generation (TT without gating) BEATS the confidence-gated version on HumanEval-R+ Top-1 (63.1 vs 62.5) and on Spearman (0.676 vs 0.650), with gating winning only on MBPP-R+ and on cost ($0.065 vs $0.077, a 16% saving). So the agreement-based confidence signal bought a 16% compute saving at a small accuracy cost -- which is quantitatively the SAME trade İşcan's ACE reports (~19% saving at a zero-harm operating point). Two independent papers converging on 'execution agreement is worth roughly a 16-19% compute saving and approximately zero accuracy' is the most reliable cross-paper regularity in this entire search, and it is a direct estimate of what our arm would deliver. No oracle, no 3B, no quantization, no single-assertion split -- it cannot be cited for a gap fraction.

title: Selection Without Signal, Recovery Through Expression: A Measurement Study of Post-Hoc Falsification Operators for Frozen Small Code Models (M. Iscan)
venue_date: arXiv preprint 2606.16999v1, 16 June 2026. Single-author, not peer-reviewed — treat as a strong prior, not settled fact.
what_it_does: Audits 26 post-hoc selection/falsification operators for FROZEN SMALL code models at a fixed pool size of k=8 on HumanEval+ and MBPP+ plus two purpose-built benchmarks, with McNemar tests and a distribution-free do-no-harm certificate. This is our experiment, already run, by someone else.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: pool k=8, T=0.8. Models: DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B, Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B, Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B (+Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B probes). Oracle-minus-BoN headroom, in TASKS: HumanEval+ (164 tasks) = 0 / 7 / 6 tasks for DS-1.3B / Qwen-1.5B / Qwen-0.5B; MBPP+ (370 tasks) = 11 / 16 / 17 tasks. Consensus-based selectors (MBR-Exec, CEMS, BTR) are reported as 'null (ties BoN)'. Max realizable consensus capture on positive-headroom cells: net <= +3 tasks, NEVER significant (p >= 0.25). Verification operators: 'null / below chance / net-negative gate'. Elimination/portfolio: 'falsified (selection artifact / FRR=0.28), delta=0'. What DID work: an expression-layer fallback that fires only when no candidate passes the visible test — DeepSeek-1.3B HumanEval+ 29->41 tasks (+12, p=2.4e-4), MBPP+ 128->161 (+33, p=1.2e-10); but only +1 to +4 tasks (ns) for the Qwen 0.5B/1.5B cells. Also an adaptive consensus early-stop: 19.1% compute saving at zero measured harm (Qwen-1.5B, n=80, Hoeffding-Bentkus p=0.0165), 63.9% saving only by accepting 2 harms (p=0.53). INFERRED: headroom as a rate = 3.0-4.6pp on MBPP+ (11-17/370) and 0-4.3pp on HumanEval+ (0-7/164) — i.e. SMALLER than our measured 7.37pp on the 3B; net <= +3 tasks = <= 0.8pp on MBPP+. INFERRED fraction of gap recovered by consensus clustering: 0 to ~19%, interval covering zero.
small_k_evidence: This is the only paper found whose headline setting IS k=8. Everything is reported at k=8.
small_model_evidence: Entirely sub-2B: DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B, Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B/1.5B, Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B. Nothing at 3B/7B, so it is one step weaker than our receivers.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the closest thing to a pre-registered null for exactly the plan under consideration: execution-agreement consensus at k=8 on small frozen code models, measured against a visible-test best-of-N baseline, recovered nothing significant. It also independently reproduces our own null on cheap post-hoc selectors. Two readings: (a) our planned agreement-clustering arm is likely to be another null, and we should not spend 22 hours on it as the headline; (b) the paper's ONE positive result is structural, not a better selector — a fallback that fires only when no candidate passes the visible assertion. That maps directly onto our 0.7169 -> 0.7455 visible-filter step and is the arm worth building. Its second positive is early STOPPING with a do-no-harm certificate (19.1% compute saving), which is literally the stopping half of our narrowed question and is achievable at our budget.

title: S*: Test Time Scaling for Code Generation (Li, Cao, Cao, Li, Tan, Keutzer, Xing, Gonzalez, Stoica; UC Berkeley)
venue_date: arXiv:2502.14382, 20 February 2025
what_it_does: Hybrid test-time scaling: parallel sampling + public-test-driven debugging, then a selection stage that clusters candidates by execution output on LLM-generated inputs and, for each cluster pair, asks the LLM to synthesise a DISTINGUISHING input, runs both candidates on it, and lets the LLM referee using the real execution results. Contains a clean head-to-head selection ablation at N=8.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, selection-method ablation at N=8 on LiveCodeBench v4, pass@1: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B: public tests 42.3, generated tests 42.3, LLM judge 42.3, adaptive input synthesis 44.5. Qwen-32B: 54.6 / 57.8 / 55.5 / 58.3. GPT-4o-mini: 54.1 / 55.2 / 56.3 / 57.3. QwQ-32B: 64.3 / 65.9 / 68.6 / 69.7. AVERAGE: public 53.8, generated tests 53.1, LLM judge 55.6, adaptive input synthesis 57.5. Main table (N=16, 2 debug rounds, LiveCodeBench v2) zero-shot -> S*: Qwen-0.5B 1.2->10.9, 1.5B 7.0->27.6, 3B 18.4->42.7, 7B 29.4->54.4, 14B 44.8->64.6, 32B 47.4->70.1. CodeContests S* vs S*-oracle: Qwen-7B 10.9 vs 12.1; Qwen-14B 21.8 vs 27.9; Qwen-32B 21.8 vs 29.7. INFERRED at N=8, Qwen-7B: model-generated tests recovered exactly 0.0pp over the visible/public test; distinguishing-input agreement recovered +2.2pp; averaged over the four models generated tests were -0.7pp (i.e. WORSE than the public test) while distinguishing inputs were +3.7pp. INFERRED: S* closes 90% of its own oracle gap on CodeContests for Qwen-7B (10.9/12.1) but only 73-78% for 14B/32B.
small_k_evidence: YES — the selection ablation is run at N=8, our exact budget. The main results are at N=16.
small_model_evidence: Qwen2.5-Coder 0.5B / 1.5B / 3B / 7B are all in the main table, so the model class matches ours. However the N=8 selection ablation is run only at 7B and above; the 0.5B-3B rows come from the full pipeline (which includes debugging with public tests), not from the selection ablation.
bearing_on_our_decision: The most important single number for us: at N=8 with a 7B receiver, MODEL-GENERATED TESTS ADDED NOTHING (42.3 -> 42.3) over the visible test, and across four models they were net negative. That is strong evidence to DROP the 'let the receiver write tests with expected outputs' arm outright. The arm that did work is the one we were actually proposing: cluster on execution outputs over generated INPUTS (no expected outputs), +2.2pp at 7B. Scaled to our gaps that is ~30% of the 3B's 7.37pp and would overshoot the 7B's 3.51pp — but S*'s referee step needs a model that can adjudicate two outputs from a distinguishing input, and a q4_k_m 3B is a poor referee, so +2.2pp is an optimistic ceiling for us, not an expectation. Note also that S*'s large small-model gains come from public-test-driven debugging, which our own audit already found LOSES to adaptive best-of-N (-0.0182, CI [-0.0260,-0.0105]) — so we should not read the 18.4->42.7 row as available to us.

title: DOCE: Finding the Sweet Spot for Execution-Based Code Generation (Li, Fernandes, Gurevych, Martins)
venue_date: arXiv:2408.13745v4, submitted 25 August 2024, last revised 16 October 2024
what_it_does: Systematic decomposition of execution-based code generation into candidate generation, n-best reranking, MBR decoding (MBR-Exec = output-agreement clustering) and self-debugging, with candidate-count and test-count scaling curves, on HumanEval+ and MBPP-S+ with open 7B-16B models.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER (Table 1, CodeLlama-7B-Instruct, n=50, T=1.6): HumanEval+ — Random 30.2, Greedy 39.0, Oracle/pass@50 76.2, Filter alone 59.7, Filter+MBR-Exec 70.1. MBPP-S+ — Random 41.9, Greedy 44.8, Oracle 72.0, Filter alone 60.8, Filter+MBR-Exec 69.3. Table 2 (n=50, with filter, MBR column): DeepSeekCoder-6.7B-Instruct HumanEval+ 90.7 / MBPP-S+ 82.1; CodeLlama-13B 76.1 / 74.7. Test-count ablation: MBR-Exec+filter peaks at 20 unit tests on HumanEval+ and at just 5 unit tests on MBPP-S+. Optimal sampling temperature 1.6-1.8 for HumanEval/MBPP (far above the usual 0.2-0.8). INFERRED, and this is the headline encouraging number: on top of the filter, MBR-Exec agreement clustering recovers (70.1-59.7)/(76.2-59.7) = 63% of the RESIDUAL oracle gap on HumanEval+ and (69.3-60.8)/(72.0-60.8) = 76% on MBPP-S+ for a 7B model. CRITICAL CAVEAT, MEASURED-IN-PAPER: the paper states it assumes access to the INPUTS of the evaluation unit tests, and its 'Filter' keeps only candidates that pass those trial tests — i.e. filtering needs real expected outputs (not available to us), and MBR-Exec's probe inputs are the benchmark's own high-quality test inputs, not model-invented ones. NOT REPORTED: how the trial tests would be generated without the benchmark, any false-accept statistics, any trivial-test filtering.
small_k_evidence: Curves are plotted from n=5 upward (5,10,15,20,25,30,40,50). Read off Figure 2 (APPROXIMATE, figure-read not table-read), CodeLlama-7B-Instruct HumanEval+: n=5 MBR ~45 / Filter ~55 / Oracle ~68; n=10 ~48 / ~58 / ~72; n=20 ~50 / ~60 / ~74. MBPP-S+: n=5 ~52 / ~58 / ~65; n=10 ~55 / ~60 / ~69; n=20 ~57 / ~61 / ~70. Do not quote these as exact.
small_model_evidence: CodeLlama-7B-Instruct and DeepSeekCoder-6.7B-Instruct are both under 8B, so the receiver scale matches ours; nothing at 3B.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the strongest pro-agreement-clustering evidence at our model scale, and it is the paper to cite if we go ahead: it says agreement clustering layered ON TOP of a pass-filter recovers 63-76% of the residual gap at 7B, and that 5 probe inputs are enough on MBPP-style tasks. But its probe inputs are the real evaluation inputs, which under our strict visible/hidden split we are forbidden from using — so DOCE measures the CEILING of our design under perfect probe inputs, not its expected value. It also tells us two cheap, actionable things: sample hotter than we probably are (T~1.6), and 5-20 probe inputs suffice, which keeps a probe-input experiment inside our 909-calls-per-hour budget.

title: Dynamic Scaling of Unit Tests for Code Reward Modeling (Ma, Zhang, Zhang, Yu, Luo, Tang) — CodeRM-8B
venue_date: arXiv:2501.01054v1, 2 January 2025
what_it_does: Trains an 8B unit-test generator (CodeRM-8B, from Llama3.1-8B) and scales the NUMBER of generated unit tests as a reward signal for best-of-100 code selection, with an explicit measurement of per-test and aggregated test quality including false-accept and false-reject rates.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, the single most directly usable table for us — individual unit-test quality on HumanEval Plus: Llama3.1-8B accuracy 60.02%, F1 44.97%, FAR 13.66%, FRR 46.13%. Llama3.1-70B accuracy 73.65%, F1 70.15%, FAR 11.10%, FRR 34.51%. CodeRM-8B accuracy 69.64%, F1 63.63%, FAR 11.17%, FRR 38.55%. With 100 tests aggregated by majority vote: Llama3.1-8B accuracy 74.21%, FAR 20.44%, FRR 30.55%; 70B accuracy 78.30%, FAR 17.19%, FRR 25.97%; CodeRM-8B accuracy 80.46%, FAR 16.48%, FRR 22.71%. Selection gains, 100 candidates: HumanEval Plus Llama3-8B 53.58 -> 72.01 (+18.43), Llama3-70B 73.74 -> 78.69 (+4.95), GPT-4o-mini 82.96 -> 86.38 (+3.42); MBPP Plus Llama3-8B 49.20 -> 66.71 (+17.51), Llama3-70B 69.33 -> 72.44 (+3.11), GPT-4o-mini 71.59 -> 75.20 (+3.61); LiveCodeBench +3.23 / +2.43 / +4.37. Scaling tests helps most on the HARDEST difficulty quintile and almost not at all on the easiest. Dynamic test-budget allocation buys ~0.5pp on MBPP Plus at fixed compute. INFERRED: a sub-8B model writing tests gets 4 out of 10 individual tests wrong (60% accuracy) and REJECTS 46% of correct programs; and aggregating more tests makes FAR WORSE (13.66% -> 20.44%) while improving FRR — i.e. more generated tests buys sensitivity by spending specificity, exactly the wrong trade for a selector that must not discard the one correct draw out of 8.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED at k<=10. All selection results are best-of-100; the test-count axis goes 1..100.
small_model_evidence: YES, and it is the cleanest such evidence found: Llama3.1-8B as a test writer is measured head-to-head against 70B, and the 8B needs ~100 tests to reach what the 70B gets from ~1. Nothing at 3B. Baseline gains are largest for the weakest POLICY model (Llama3-8B +18.43pp), which is the one encouraging signal for weak receivers.
bearing_on_our_decision: Quantifies the false-accept/false-reject question the angle asked for, at a model size one step above our 3B. FRR 46% is the killer for us: with only k=8 draws and a 3B-quality test writer, a selector that rejects nearly half of correct programs will frequently discard the only passing draw, which is precisely how a selector goes NEGATIVE — and our own audit already saw negative recovered fractions (-0.18, -0.06). The +18.43pp for the weakest policy is not transferable: it required 100 candidates, ~100 generated tests and a FINE-TUNED 8B test generator, i.e. roughly 20k receiver calls per run at our throughput (~22 contended hours) before any tuning. Verdict: do not build a test-generation arm; if any generated signal is used, use INPUTS only and never trust a generated expected output.

title: Benchmarking LLMs for Unit Test Generation from Real-World Functions (Huang, Zhang, Harman, Zhang, Du, Ng) — UnLeakedTestBench (ULT) / PreLeakedTestbench (PLT)
venue_date: arXiv:2508.00408v1, 4 August 2025
what_it_does: Builds a matched pair of test-generation benchmarks: ULT (3,909 real-world function-level tasks with no detected training overlap) and PLT (the same task format but drawn from functions known to be in training data), so the memorization contribution to test-generation performance can be measured directly.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, the answer to the leakage-hazard question: at K=5 queries, ULT vs PLT — Pass@5 12.57% vs 44.45% (a 31.88 percentage-point gap); line coverage 45.10% vs 55.13% (-10.03pp); branch coverage 30.22% vs 40.07% (-9.85pp); mutation score 40.21% vs 50.80% (-10.59pp). Best on ULT pass@1: Gemma-3-27b-it and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct at 17.83%. Worst: Phi-4-mini-instruct at 8.52%. 12 models evaluated, including sub-8B: CodeLlama-7B-Instruct, Seed-Coder-8B-Instruct, Gemma-3-4b-it, DeepSeek-Coder-1.3b-instruct, Phi-4-mini-instruct, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct; plus DeepSeek-Coder-6.7b/33b, Qwen2.5-Coder-14B/32B, Gemma-3-12b/27b. INFERRED: test-generation ability is inflated by a factor of ~3.5x (44.45/12.57) when the target function was in training data; on genuinely unseen functions even a 32B model writes a fully-passing test suite for fewer than 1 task in 5.
small_k_evidence: K=5 queries per task is the headline setting — small-k for the TEST-GENERATION side, which is the side we care about.
small_model_evidence: Five of the twelve models are under 8B (down to DeepSeek-Coder-1.3b and Gemma-3-4b), and the worst performer is the small Phi-4-mini at 8.52% pass@1 on unleaked tasks.
bearing_on_our_decision: This is the measurement the angle asked for and nobody else supplies: when a model writes tests for a task it has memorised, its tests look ~32pp better than they really are. MBPP and HumanEval are exactly the memorised class (see arXiv:2403.04811, arXiv:2407.07565). Therefore ANY positive result we obtain from model-written tests on MBPP-sanitized + HumanEval is confounded by leakage and would not survive a reviewer, let alone transfer. Two consequences: (1) a generated-test arm on our benchmark is scientifically uninterpretable, which is an independent reason to drop it beyond its measured 0.0pp gain in S*; (2) cross-candidate EXECUTION AGREEMENT over generated INPUTS is leakage-IMMUNE in the relevant sense — it never asks the model for an expected output, so a memorised answer cannot be smuggled into the selection criterion. That asymmetry is the cleanest scientific argument for the agreement-clustering design over the test-generation design, and it is worth stating explicitly in the writeup.

title: Semantic Voting: Execution-Grounded Consensus for LLM Code Generation (Jiang, Yi, Zhu)
what_it_does: Isolates the probe-INPUT generation question for agreement clustering: an LLM emits K=10 abstract input 'sketches' (empty list, sorted-with-duplicates, ...), each instantiated M=5 times for D=50 concrete inputs; candidates are clustered by execution signature and the plurality cluster wins. Ablates input STRATEGY (sketch vs direct-LLM vs type-aware random fuzzing vs example-only) and input COUNT, and reports cluster geometry.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER. Input-strategy ablation, HumanEval+, N=100, pass@1 (Pro-Low / Flash-Med / Lite-Low): sketch 99.3 / 97.2 / 95.1; direct LLM 97.8 / 95.8 / 94.5; type-aware random 94.2 / 89.4 / 93.9; example-only 95.0 / 86.6 / 90.9. Sketch beats direct LLM by 0.6-2.1pp and beats random/example-only by up to 11.3pp. Input-COUNT scaling (Flash-Medium): D=5 95.1% pass@1, 1.20 clusters/problem, largest cluster 48.5/50; D=10 96.3%, 1.28, 47.8; D=20 96.3%, 1.34, 47.6; D=30 97.0%, 1.38, 47.4; D=50 97.0%, 1.43, 47.2 — gains saturate past D=30, and 'even five well-chosen inputs already exceed output-pattern majority voting by 29 pp'. Cluster geometry on HumanEval+: 1.2-1.5 clusters per problem, largest cluster typically 38-48 of 50 candidates; selection failure 1.5-2.7%, generation failure 2.8-3.9% (generation, not selection, is the bottleneck). Aggregator equivalence: SemanticVote vs MBR-Exec differ by only -1.22 to +0.61pp across all 18 configurations, and SemanticVote vs weighted voting by +/-0.79pp, none significant. Main results N=50, sketch inputs: HumanEval+ Pro-Low 98.8 vs majority-voting 75.0; Flash-Med 96.3 vs 65.9; Lite-Low 92.1 vs 51.8; MBPP+ Pro-Low 97.4 vs 77.2; Flash-Med 91.8 vs 51.3; Lite-Low 90.7 vs 39.4. INFERRED: the choice of AGGREGATOR is worth ~1pp while the choice of INPUT GENERATOR is worth up to 11.3pp, so ~90% of the engineering value in agreement clustering sits in input generation. Also INFERRED: with 1.2-1.5 clusters per problem and 47/50 candidates in the plurality cluster, agreement clustering is near-degenerate for strong models — it ranks almost nothing, it merely confirms the majority.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED below N=50 for candidates; the INPUT-count axis does go down to D=5, which is the axis that matters for our compute budget.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED — Gemini 3.1 Pro / 3 Flash / 3.1 Flash Lite only, all frontier-class, and the headline pass@1 values sit at 91-99%, i.e. saturated. Nothing at or under 8B, nothing quantized, nothing local.
bearing_on_our_decision: Answers the probe-input half of our angle cleanly, and the answer is actionable: use type-CLASS sketches (empty, singleton, duplicates, boundary, degenerate) instantiated a few times each, not raw type-aware fuzzing and not the docstring example — the last two are worth up to 11.3pp less. D=5-10 inputs is enough, which costs us roughly one extra receiver call per task (~230-500 calls, under one hour), so this is cheap to falsify. It also hands us the honest deflation: the paper's huge headline margins are against a TEXT-majority-voting baseline, not against a visible-test filter, so they are not comparable to our 0.7455 baseline; and its cluster geometry (plurality cluster = 94% of candidates) says clustering has little to rank when candidates agree. At k=8 with a q4_k_m 3B our candidates will disagree more, so we will see more clusters — but each cluster's plurality estimate rests on 8 draws, where a 2-vs-3 split is statistical noise. Expect wide intervals; power, not signal, may be the binding constraint.

title: CodeT: Code Generation with Generated Tests (Chen, Lian, Wang, Fu, Wei, Chen, Duan et al.; Microsoft Research)
venue_date: arXiv:2207.10397, July 2022; published at ICLR 2023 (OpenReview ktrw68Cmu9c)
what_it_does: The origin of the whole line: the model writes its own assertions, candidates are executed against them, and 'dual execution agreement' scores a candidate by the number of tests it passes TIMES the number of other candidates with the identical pass/fail signature — i.e. test-based voting fused with output-agreement clustering.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, pass@1 baseline -> CodeT. HumanEval: code-cushman-001 33.5 -> 44.5; code-davinci-001 39.0 -> 50.2; code-davinci-002 47.0 -> 65.8; InCoder-6B 16.4 -> 20.6; CodeGen-Mono-16B 29.7 -> 36.7. MBPP: code-cushman-001 45.9 -> 55.4; code-davinci-001 51.8 -> 61.9; code-davinci-002 58.1 -> 67.7; InCoder-6B 21.3 -> 34.4; CodeGen-Mono-16B 42.4 -> 49.5. APPS (davinci-002): intro 27.2 -> 34.6, interview 5.1 -> 8.1, competition 1.8 -> 2.2. CodeContests 0.7 -> 2.1. Oracle pass@100 (davinci-002): HumanEval 92.1, MBPP 84.5, CodeContests 7.5. Oracle pass@100 for the small/open models: InCoder-6B HumanEval 47.5, MBPP 66.2; CodeGen-Mono-16B HumanEval 73.7, MBPP 79.1. Budget: n=100 code samples and up to ~500 extracted assertions per problem on HumanEval/MBPP; 1000 samples on CodeContests. Assertions-per-sample ablation (davinci-002, HumanEval): limit=1 -> 56.5, limit=3 -> 62.9, limit=5 -> 65.8. Test-case quality: Codex models exceed 95% test accuracy (canonical solution passes) and 95%+ statement / 98%+ branch coverage, while CodeGen reaches only 78.2% statement coverage and InCoder/CodeGen have markedly lower accuracy and higher 'toxicity' (false-accept) rates; the paper states CodeT's gain tracks test-case quality across models. Leakage discipline, MEASURED-IN-PAPER: 'we remove all example input-output cases from the context before generating code solutions and test cases, to avoid exposing real test cases to the language model.' INFERRED fraction of oracle gap recovered at n=100: InCoder-6B HumanEval (20.6-16.4)/(47.5-16.4) = 13.5%; InCoder-6B MBPP (34.4-21.3)/(66.2-21.3) = 29.2%; CodeGen-16B HumanEval (36.7-29.7)/(73.7-29.7) = 15.9%; CodeGen-16B MBPP (49.5-42.4)/(79.1-42.4) = 19.3%; davinci-002 HumanEval (65.8-47.0)/(92.1-47.0) = 41.7%; MBPP (67.7-58.1)/(84.5-58.1) = 36.4%. The sub-16B open models recover 13-29% of the gap; the frontier model of its day recovers 36-42%.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED at k<=10 candidates. The paper's small-budget ablation is over TESTS (limit=1 assertion per sample -> 56.5 vs 65.8 at limit=5), not over candidates, and it keeps n=100 candidates throughout. A reported sample-count table exists but the values we extracted were non-monotone and we do not trust them enough to quote.
small_model_evidence: InCoder-6B is the only sub-8B model, and it is the WORST case in the paper: +4.2pp on HumanEval against a 31.1pp oracle gap (13.5% recovered). Its test-case accuracy and coverage are explicitly called out as much lower than Codex's.
bearing_on_our_decision: Sets the honest prior for the family: the canonical method, given 100 candidates and ~500 self-written assertions — roughly 60x our per-task budget — recovers only 13-29% of the oracle gap for sub-16B models, and the paper itself attributes the shortfall to test quality. Scaled to our 3B's 7.37pp gap, 13-29% is 0.010-0.021, which is inside the noise band our audits already produce on 448 tasks. CodeT also validates our grading design by doing the same thing for the same reason (stripping visible examples to avoid exposing real tests), and its limit=1 result is a warning: our MBPP tasks expose exactly ONE visible assertion, which is the degenerate end of its test-count curve.

title: B4: Towards Optimal Assessment of Plausible Code Solutions with Plausible Tests (Chen, Liu, Tao, Hong, Lo, Xia, Sun)
venue_date: arXiv:2409.08692; ASE 2024 (39th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering), DOI 10.1145/3691620.3695536
what_it_does: Treats selection under UNRELIABLE tests as Bayesian inference: it models the joint posterior over which solutions and which tests are correct given the observed solution-by-test pass matrix, and approximates the optimal selection with four Beta functions plus integer programming. The principled upper end of what any code-vs-test agreement scheme can extract.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, pass@1 on discriminative problems (Table 1): HumanEval/CodeGen — random 32.5, MaxPass 28.6, MBR-exec 44.8, CodeT 51.5, B4 56.8-58.0. HumanEval/Codex — random 39.2, MaxPass 57.8, MBR-exec 55.0, CodeT 71.7, B4 70.6-73.1. MBPP/CodeGen — random 42.4, MaxPass 48.1, MBR-exec 56.4, CodeT 64.9, B4 64.7-66.7. MBPP/Codex — random 55.1, MaxPass 70.5, MBR-exec 71.9, CodeT 80.0, B4 80.8-81.9. APPS-intro/Codex — random 36.2, MaxPass 46.4, MBR-exec 41.6, CodeT 59.5, B4 63.7-64.4. Headline: up to +50% relative over the strongest heuristic and +246% over random in the hardest scenarios; +6.1-7.5% relative over CodeT on discriminative problems, +10.1-12.0% on hard problems (solution pass rate below 0.5). Budget: 100 solutions and 100 tests per problem (50 each on APPS). Models: Codex (code-davinci-002), CodeGen-16B-Python, StarCoder, CodeLlama-7B-Python, DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct. A simulated study (Figure 5) varies N from about 5 to 30 solutions and reports B4 ahead of MaxPass and CodeT at every scale. INFERRED: MBR-exec (pure output-agreement clustering) is consistently BEATEN by test-based CodeT here — by 6.7pp on HumanEval/CodeGen, 16.7pp on HumanEval/Codex, 8.5pp on MBPP/CodeGen, 8.1pp on MBPP/Codex, 17.9pp on APPS-intro — which is the opposite ordering from S* at N=8. The difference is budget: with 100 self-written tests, tests win; with 8 candidates and no reliable tests, they do not.
small_k_evidence: Partially: the SIMULATION sweeps N from ~5 to ~30 solutions and B4 stays ahead of MaxPass and CodeT throughout. The real-data tables are all at 100 solutions / 100 tests. Exact small-N values: NOT REPORTED.
small_model_evidence: CodeLlama-7B-Python and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct are both under 8B and are in the model list, but the main comparison tables we could extract report only CodeGen and Codex rows; per-model numbers for the sub-8B models: NOT FOUND.
bearing_on_our_decision: If we run any code-vs-test agreement arm, B4 is the baseline we must beat, not CodeT — and it is cheap to add, since it is a closed-form posterior over the same pass matrix we would already have computed, costing zero extra receiver calls. It also supplies the right framing for our writeup: the problem is jointly estimating solution and test correctness from an 8x(few) pass matrix, and at that size the posterior will be nearly flat, which is a principled explanation for why our cross-fitted models recovered nothing. Its explicit finding that gains concentrate on HARD problems (pass rate below 0.5, +10-12% relative) also validates restricting to our 230-task informative difficulty band.

title: ACES: Who Tests the Tests? Leave-One-Out AUC Consistency for Code Generation (Sun, Zhang, Xie, Liu, Du, Li, Li)
venue_date: arXiv:2604.03922v2, submitted 5 April 2026, revised 12 July 2026
what_it_does: Attacks the circularity in test-based selection (knowing which tests are good requires knowing which code is correct) by holding out one test, ranking candidates on the rest, and measuring whether the held-out test's pass/fail pattern agrees with that ranking — a leave-one-out AUC that provably tracks a test's ability to separate correct from incorrect code. Yields per-test weights (ACES-C closed form, ACES-O optimised).
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, pass@1 (HumanEval / HumanEval+ / MBPP): majority voting 80.49 / 69.51 / 68.62; CodeT 78.05 / 67.87 / 71.90; MBR-exec 72.96 / 62.12 / 70.79; ACES-C 82.93 / 71.34 / 71.19; ACES-O 84.15 / 74.39 / 72.37. Budget ~200 candidates and ~500 generated tests per problem, generator GPT-3.5-Turbo; HumanEval 164, HumanEval+ 164, MBPP 427 problems. TEST-QUALITY measurements, which is why this paper matters to us: on MBPP 17.3% of generated tests are false-positive-inducing and 26.3% are 'misleading', versus 9.5% and 18.8% on HumanEval; ACES-C's weights correctly identify at least 94.8% of informative tests; misidentifications cluster at discriminative power delta_j near 0. INFERRED: MBPP's generated tests are ~1.8x more false-positive-prone and ~1.4x more misleading than HumanEval's, with a strong frontier-class generator — so our MBPP-sanitized majority, graded by a q4_k_m 3B's own tests, sits at the bad end of a bad distribution. INFERRED: MBR-exec output-agreement is the WORST of the five selectors on HumanEval (72.96, i.e. 7.5pp below plain majority voting) and roughly ties it on MBPP.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED in the sense we need. The paper reports pass@k only for k in {1,2,5} as an evaluation metric; the CANDIDATE pool is ~200 throughout and the test pool ~500. There is no small-candidate-budget experiment.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED — GPT-3.5-Turbo generates both code and tests. No sub-8B model, no local or quantized model.
bearing_on_our_decision: Two things. First, it supplies the measured false-accept numbers the angle asked for, on MBPP specifically (17.3% false-positive tests, 26.3% misleading) from a generator far stronger than our receivers — a lower bound on the noise we would inject. Second, it is a caution against the pure-clustering plan: with a competent generator and a large pool, MBR-exec was the weakest method tested, 7.5pp below simple majority voting on HumanEval. Its LOO-AUC idea is nevertheless the one piece of statistical machinery here that fits our constraint of known propensities and would cost no extra receiver calls, but at k=8 with a handful of probe inputs the leave-one-out AUC per test is estimated from 8 binary outcomes and will be essentially unidentifiable. Worth citing as related work; not worth implementing at our budget.

title: Large Language Models as Test Case Generators: Performance Evaluation and Enhancement (Li, Yuan; Beihang University)
what_it_does: Directly measures how often LLM-written test cases are simply WRONG (the assertion fails on the ground-truth solution), across a weak-to-strong model ladder, on prompts with the docstring examples deliberately stripped out; then proposes TestChain (decoupled input generation and output computation, with a Python interpreter in the loop) as a fix.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, fraction of generated test cases that are INCORRECT (fail on the ground-truth solution), 1-shot baseline. HumanEval-no-exp (164 problems, up to 820 test cases): StarChat-beta 58.90%, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct 32.93%, GPT-3.5-turbo 25.98%, GPT-4-turbo 15.37%. LeetCode-no-exp (39 problems, up to 195 test cases): StarChat 87.69%, CodeLlama-13B 71.28%, GPT-3.5 61.03%, GPT-4 42.05%. Assertion errors (wrong expected output) dominate the error mix, ahead of runtime errors and timeouts. TestChain lifts GPT-4 on LeetCode-no-exp from 57.95% to 71.79% accuracy (+13.84pp). Mutation-based bug detection: GPT-4 83.11% on HumanEval; coverage falls sharply for weaker models on harder problems. LEAKAGE, MEASURED-IN-PAPER: the authors state LLMs may plagiarise the test-case examples included in the prompt and therefore construct HumanEval-no-exp and LeetCode-no-exp with all examples removed. INFERRED: the incorrect-assertion rate scales almost monotonically with model weakness — 15.4% (GPT-4) -> 26.0% (GPT-3.5) -> 32.9% (13B) -> 58.9% (StarChat) on HumanEval, i.e. roughly a 4x degradation from frontier to weak open model, and it roughly DOUBLES again on harder (LeetCode) problems for every model.
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED — no candidate-selection experiment at all, so no k axis.
small_model_evidence: Partially: CodeLlama-13B-Instruct at 32.93% incorrect and StarChat-beta at 58.90% incorrect are the weak end, but both are at or above 13B. NOT REPORTED below 13B. Extrapolating the ladder, a q4_k_m 3B would be expected to produce a MAJORITY of wrong assertions on HumanEval-class tasks, but that extrapolation is ours, not the paper's.
bearing_on_our_decision: Puts a number on the premise of the whole angle: at 13B, one third of self-written assertions are wrong, and at StarChat quality, nearly six in ten. A selector built on assertions that are wrong a third to a half of the time cannot be expected to recover a 3.5-7.4pp gap from 8 draws. It also independently confirms the leakage hazard at the mechanism level — the authors had to strip docstring examples because models plagiarise them — which for us means that a 3B asked to write tests for an MBPP task will very often just regurgitate the single visible assertion, producing a selector that is definitionally identical to the 0.7455 visible-verdict baseline we already have. That is the most likely failure mode of a generated-test arm and it is predictable in advance, which is a reason not to spend the compute discovering it.

title: CoSPlay: Cooperative Self-Play at Test-Time with Self-Generated Code and Unit Test (Hu, Liu, Huang, Li, Yang, Wu, Zhong, Yang, Yue)
venue_date: arXiv:2605.23491, submitted 22 May 2026, revised 25 May 2026
what_it_does: Training-free, ground-truth-free co-evolution of a code pool and a unit-test pool from the same model: bidirectional pass counts in the code-by-test execution matrix prune or repair weak code and refresh unreliable tests, and then — the part that matters to us — output-consensus clustering over model-generated random valid INPUTS breaks ties among candidates that are level on pass count.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct averaged over four benchmarks (LiveBench 128, LiveCodeBench v2 511, CodeContests 239, CodeForces 467 = 1,345 problems): Signal 22.1 -> 31.9, UNIT-TEST ACCURACY 14.6% -> 78.3%, code accuracy 19.0 -> 23.3, BoN 22.1 -> 33.2. Contribution of the clustering step alone: average BoN 24.4 -> 33.2 (+8.8pp); LiveBench BoN 42.7 -> 50.3 (+7.6pp); CodeContests BoN 25.1 -> 32.6 (+7.5pp). Beats CURE-7B, which was RL-trained on 4.5k ground-truth test cases, on average BoN (33.2 vs 32.9) with far better test accuracy (78.3 vs 54.9). Applied to CURE-7B, +5.7pp. Probe inputs, MEASURED-IN-PAPER: the model is prompted for R random VALID inputs 'which do not require outputs' — exactly the leakage-immune probe-input design. Budget N=16 code and N=16 test pool, scalability studies to 64. Input-count ablation: clustering inputs swept k=0 to 64, with the paper reporting that more inputs generally improve or stabilise accuracy because a longer execution signature separates true functional equivalence from spurious agreement, with the clearest gains on LiveBench and LiveCodeBench; exact per-k values NOT FOUND in the text we could extract. Oracle/pass@N upper bound: NOT REPORTED. INFERRED: a 7B model's self-written unit tests start at 14.6% accuracy on competition-class problems — far below the ~60-70% seen on HumanEval-class tasks — and the tie-break-only use of clustering means the +8.8pp is measured on top of a pass-count filter, which is the same layering as DOCE and the same layering we would use.
small_k_evidence: N=16 is the headline budget, twice ours; the input-count axis reaches down to k=0. NOT REPORTED at N=8.
small_model_evidence: YES at the 7B/8B boundary: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Coder, Seed-Coder-8B-Instruct, plus 14B-16B and frontier models. Our 7B receiver is in-class; our 3B is not, and nothing is quantized.
bearing_on_our_decision: The most architecturally aligned paper found: it uses generated INPUTS only (no expected outputs, hence leakage-immune), it applies clustering as a TIE-BREAK on top of a pass-count filter rather than as a standalone ranker, and it does so at 7B. Its +8.8pp for the clustering step is the most optimistic same-scale estimate available, and it says more probe inputs monotonically help. Two deflations before we believe it: the benchmarks are competition-class where oracle headroom is enormous and a weak selector has room to be right by luck, whereas our 230-task band has 3.5-7.4pp of headroom total; and the +8.8pp is measured after the self-play repair loop, which our own audit found loses to adaptive best-of-N. The transferable design lesson stands: ask the 3B for INPUTS, never for expected outputs, and use the cluster only to break ties among candidates that already pass the visible assertion.

title: Inference Scaling fLaws: The Limits of LLM Resampling with Imperfect Verifiers (Stroebl, Kapoor, Narayanan; Princeton)
venue_date: arXiv:2411.17501, submitted 26 November 2024, latest version 26 March 2026
what_it_does: Proves and measures the ceiling on resampling-based inference scaling when the verifier is imperfect: because resampling cannot reduce the probability that a wrong program passes the verifier, the false-positive rate of the verifier imposes a hard upper bound on achievable accuracy regardless of compute.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: on HumanEval and MBPP, whose unit tests have limited coverage, there is a strong correlation between a model's single-sample accuracy and its FALSE POSITIVE rate — weaker models produce wrong programs that pass the visible tests more often. Consequence stated by the authors: no amount of inference scaling of a weaker model lets it match the single-sample accuracy of a sufficiently strong model. Exact per-model false-positive rates and the numeric ceilings: NOT FOUND in the material we could retrieve (the abstract and summary state the correlation and the bound without the table values).
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED as a k-sweep with numbers; the argument is asymptotic in the budget, which makes it a statement about the k -> large limit rather than about k=8. Its practical import at k=8 is that the ceiling binds even earlier, since fewer draws means less chance of a true positive while the false-positive probability per draw is unchanged.
small_model_evidence: The correlation between weak single-sample accuracy and high false-positive rate is the paper's central empirical claim, and it is measured on HumanEval and MBPP, which is our benchmark pair. Specific sub-8B model rows: NOT FOUND.
bearing_on_our_decision: The theoretical frame for why our audit came out the way it did, and why the remaining gap may be structurally rather than accidentally unrecoverable. Any selector we can build is an imperfect verifier; its false-positive rate is bounded below by the quality of the signal it sees (one visible assertion, or a handful of self-generated probe inputs), and our receivers are exactly the weak models for which false-positive rates are measured to be highest. This is the paper to cite for the negative result if agreement clustering also comes out null: the finding would then be an instance of a known bound, not an implementation failure, which makes a null publishable rather than merely disappointing. It also argues for reframing the contribution around STOPPING — where the bound does not bite, because a do-no-harm early stop is evaluated on compute saved at fixed accuracy, not on accuracy gained.

title: Improving Code Generation via Small Language Model-as-a-judge (Crupi, Tufano, Bavota)
venue_date: arXiv:2602.11911, 13 February 2026; ICSE 2026 (48th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Software Engineering), DOI 10.1145/3744916.3787822
what_it_does: Uses SMALL language models as judges to pick among a handful of candidates generated by a small model, and compares that against log-likelihood selection and random selection, precisely in the k = 2 to 10 range.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER, Qwen2.5-Coder 3B as generator, pass@1: single candidate 0.361; k=2 with judge 0.443; k=5 with judge 0.495; k=10 with judge 0.521. At k=10 the judge beats log-likelihood selection 0.521 vs 0.397 and random 0.521 vs 0.377. The 3B-plus-judge team at k=10 reportedly matches or exceeds the corresponding 33B model's standalone pass@1, described as a 15.6% boost for Qwen2.5-Coder 3B. No execution and no generated tests are used — the signal is purely the judge model reading the candidates. Oracle pass@k upper bound: NOT REPORTED, so a fraction-of-gap cannot be computed. INFERRED: the incremental value per doubling of k shrinks fast — +0.082 going 1->2, +0.052 going 2->5, +0.026 going 5->10 — so at k=8 the judge is worth roughly +0.14 to +0.15 over a single attempt, most of which is the raw benefit of having more draws rather than of judging well; and the judge's margin over RANDOM at k=10 is +0.144, which is the part attributable to selection.
small_k_evidence: YES, and it is the only paper found that reports k = 2, 5, 10 explicitly as its main axis. This is our regime on the k axis.
small_model_evidence: YES — Qwen2.5-Coder 3B is the generator and the judges are also small models. This is the closest match to our 3B receiver of anything found, though it is unquantized and the benchmark is not MBPP/HumanEval-sanitized.
bearing_on_our_decision: The single most important comparator for us on BOTH axes at once: small model, small k. It demonstrates that SOMETHING recovers a large selection margin at k<=10 with a 3B-class model — +0.144 over random at k=10 — which means our own null is not a law of nature at this scale. But note what the winning signal is: a model READING the candidates, not static features (which failed for us) and not execution agreement. It also shows log-likelihood selection, the closest analogue to our cheap-feature models, at 0.397 versus random 0.377 — a mere +0.02, consistent with our recovered fractions of -0.18 to 0.00. So the literature's verdict at our scale is: cheap surface signals give nothing, a judging pass gives a lot. Against our constraints, an 8-candidate judging pass costs one extra receiver call per task (~230-500 calls, well under an hour) — comparable to the probe-input plan and cheaper than anything test-based. This should be run as the control arm alongside agreement clustering, because if the judge works and clustering does not, the paper writes itself; and because its absence would be the first question a reviewer asks.

title: Is Your Code Generated by ChatGPT Really Correct? Rigorous Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code Generation (Liu, Xia, Wang, Zhang) — EvalPlus / HumanEval+
venue_date: arXiv:2305.01210; NeurIPS 2023 (poster 72990)
what_it_does: Defines the standard for PROBE-INPUT generation in this literature: an LLM produces high-quality seed inputs from the problem description, then those seeds are recursively mutated in a TYPE-AWARE fashion (flip booleans, insert/remove list elements, perturb strings) to expand coverage, with test-suite minimisation afterwards. This is the machinery any agreement-clustering probe-input generator should reuse.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: HumanEval+ adds 80x more unique test cases than HumanEval and corrects wrong ground truths. Across 26 evaluated LLMs, pass@k on HumanEval+ is up to 19.3-28.9% lower than on HumanEval depending on k. INFERRED: the 19.3-28.9% pass@k collapse is a direct measurement of how much of apparent correctness is an artifact of THIN probe inputs, i.e. how much discriminative power the type-aware mutation layer adds over the benchmark's original handful of cases. Per-model pass@1 reductions and any saturation curve over the number of inputs: NOT FOUND in the material retrieved; the input-count saturation question is better answered by arXiv:2605.08680 (D=5 to 50) and arXiv:2408.13745 (5-20 tests).
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED — this is a benchmark-construction paper, not a selection paper, so there is no candidate-budget axis.
small_model_evidence: NOT REPORTED as a size analysis, though several of the 26 evaluated models are small open models; no per-size breakdown of the probe-input effect was found.
bearing_on_our_decision: Two uses. First, methodological: if we build probe inputs, the accepted recipe is LLM seed plus type-aware mutation, and we can generate the mutations with plain Python rather than receiver calls — which means the probe-input arm costs almost nothing against our 909-calls-per-hour budget, since mutation is free and only the seeds need the model. Second, it is the reason our strict visible/hidden split is defensible: EvalPlus showed that the original HumanEval/MBPP cases are thin enough that up to 28.9% of apparent pass@k is illusory, so grading on a held-out hidden suite (as we do) is the correct design and our 0.8192 oracle is a more honest ceiling than a HumanEval-original oracle would be.

title: Competition-Level Code Generation with AlphaCode (Li, Choi, Chung, Kushman, Schrittwieser, Leblond et al.; DeepMind)
venue_date: arXiv:2203.07814, March 2022; published in Science 378(6624):1092-1097, December 2022
what_it_does: The original large-scale use of execution-agreement clustering as a selection mechanism, and the origin of the dedicated probe-input GENERATOR: a separate model is trained to emit plausible (not necessarily correct) inputs given a problem description and example I/O, candidates are executed on those inputs, and programs with identical output signatures are grouped, with the largest clusters submitted first.
key_numbers: MEASURED-IN-PAPER: clustering uses 50 generated test inputs and up to 8,192 model samples (both tuned on validation) for all reported clustering results. In the cumulative ablation taking a 1.1B base model from 15.2% to 24.1% 10@100k solve rate, CLUSTERING contributes +2.6pp — the largest single contribution in the ladder (MLM +1.8, tempering +1.7, metadata/ratings +0.6, value conditioning +0.9, GOLD +1.3, clustering +2.6). INFERRED: +2.6pp on a base of ~21.5pp is a ~12% relative improvement, bought with 50 probe inputs and a candidate pool of 100,000 samples filtered down to 10 submissions. INFERRED cost ratio: AlphaCode spent ~10^4 candidates per submitted answer; we have 8. Fraction of any oracle gap closed: NOT REPORTED (the paper reports solve rate at a submission budget, not pass@n oracle).
small_k_evidence: NOT REPORTED, and it is the extreme opposite: 8,192 to 100,000 samples per problem. The probe-input count, 50, is the only quantity in our range.
small_model_evidence: The base model in the ablation ladder is 1.1B, which is small by parameter count, but it is a specialised competition-code model sampling 100k times per problem, so the compute regime is nothing like ours. The probe-input generator is a separate trained model, which we cannot replicate.
bearing_on_our_decision: Establishes two things we can use and one we cannot. Usable: 50 probe inputs was enough for DeepMind at 8,192 candidates, which corroborates the 5-20 range found by DOCE and the D=5-30 saturation found by Semantic Voting — so probe-input COUNT is not where our risk lies. Also usable as calibration: even at 100,000 candidates with a purpose-trained input generator, clustering bought only +2.6pp absolute. Not usable: the dedicated trained input-generation model. The honest reading for our design is that clustering is a real but small effect that has never been demonstrated to be large, and that its measured magnitude at massive scale (+2.6pp) is the same order as our entire 7B selection gap (3.51pp) — so we should power the experiment to detect a couple of points, not expect to close the gap.
